cards.front: What does the javac command do with a .java source file?
cards.back: Reads class/interface definitions and compiles them to bytecode class files
cards.extra: Unlike java, which launches code, javac produces the .class file. It can also process annotations in source files and classes.
cards.example:
javac MyClass.java
# javac reads class/interface definitions and compiles them to bytecode class files

cards.front: What file name does javac produce for a class MyClass declared in MyClass.java?
cards.extra: Source and class files must share a root name identifying the class. Inner classes get extra names joining outer and inner, e.g. MyClass$MyInnerClass.class.
cards.example:
javac MyClass.java   # writes MyClass.class
java MyClass         # runs the compiled class

cards.front: Where does javac place a class file by default?
cards.back: In the same directory as the source file
cards.extra: To redirect output you pass -d directory. For a packaged class com.mypackage.MyClass compiled with -d /home/myclasses, the result is /home/myclasses/com/mypackage/MyClass.class.
cards.example:
javac src/MyClass.java   # MyClass.class written beside MyClass.java
javac MyClass.java       # MyClass.class written beside this source too

cards.front: Which javac option sets the destination directory for class files, creating package subdirectories as needed?
cards.extra: Because the package name becomes a subdirectory path under the destination, you do not pre-create the package folders. Without -d, class files land next to their sources.
cards.example:
javac -d out src/p/App.java
find out -name '*.class'   # out/p/App.class: -d creates package dirs

cards.front: How do you hand javac a long list of source files without typing them all on the command line?
cards.back: Put them in a file and pass it as @filename
cards.extra: An argument file can mix options and source file names, separated by spaces or newlines. It lets you build commands of almost any length, though OS limits still apply.
cards.example:
# sources.txt lists App.java, Util.java, ... one per line
javac @sources.txt

cards.front: In a javac @argfile, how are paths of the file names listed inside the argument file resolved?
cards.back: Relative to the current working directory, not the argfile's location
cards.extra: Wildcards such as *.java are not allowed in argument files, recursive @ expansion is unsupported, and -J options are not allowed because they are passed to the launcher.
cards.example:
# run from the project root, not from the directory holding files.txt
javac @sources/files.txt   # App.java inside the file resolves in the project root

cards.front: Which javac option reads options and file names from a file?
cards.extra: You can pass several argument files. Options such as -J are excluded because they go to the launcher, which does not support argument files.
cards.example:
# opts.txt: -d out and App.java, separated by whitespace
javac @opts.txt   # reads options and file names from that file

cards.front: Which environment variable does javac prepend to its command line, introduced in JDK 9?
cards.extra: Its whitespace-separated content is prepended to the arguments passed to javac. Quotes can enclose arguments containing spaces, @files are supported there, but wildcards are not.
cards.example:
export JDK_JAVAC_OPTIONS="-encoding UTF-8"
javac App.java   # -encoding UTF-8 is prepended to this command by javac

cards.front: What is the default user class path for javac when -class-path/-cp is not specified?
cards.extra: If -sourcepath is not set, the class path is also searched for source files, and if -processorpath is not set, it is searched for annotation processors too.
cards.example:
javac Hello.java         # with no -cp, the user class path is the current directory
javac -cp . Hello.java   # the same, explicitly

cards.front: Which option makes javac show a description of each use of a deprecated member instead of a summary?
cards.extra: Without it, javac only summarises which source files use deprecated members. The option is shorthand for -Xlint:deprecation.
cards.example:
javac -deprecation MyClass.java
# -deprecation shows a description of each use of a deprecated member instead of a summary

cards.front: What does javac -g generate compared with the default?
cards.extra: By default javac emits only line-number and source-file information. -g:none emits no debug info; -g:[lines,vars,source] selects individual kinds.
cards.example:
javac -g MyClass.java   # all debugging info, including local variables
javac MyClass.java      # default: less debug info

cards.front: What does javac -g:none do?
cards.extra: It is the opposite end from plain -g, which emits everything. Selective generation uses -g:lines, -g:vars, and -g:source in a comma-separated list.
cards.example:
javac -g App.java       # all debugging information
javac -g:none App.java  # generates no debugging information

cards.front: What does javac -parameters record in the generated class file?
cards.back: The formal parameter names of constructors and methods
cards.extra: They become retrievable through java.lang.reflect.Executable.getParameters(). Without the flag, reflection sees only synthetic names like arg0.
cards.example:
javac -parameters MyClass.java
# -parameters records the formal parameter names of constructors and methods in the class file

cards.front: What does javac -proc:none do?
cards.extra: Its sibling -proc:only runs only the annotation processors and skips compilation. Processors are otherwise discovered via META-INF/services/javax.annotation.processing.Processor.
cards.example:
javac -proc:none MyClass.java   # compiles without annotation processing
javac MyClass.java              # default: annotation processing may run

cards.front: Which javac option bypasses the default discovery process and names the annotation processors to run?
cards.extra: By default processors are located through service-provider configuration files named META-INF/services/javax.annotation.processing.Processor on the search path.
cards.example:
javac -processor my.Proc1,my.Proc2 MyClass.java
# names processors explicitly; no default discovery

cards.front: Why does the javac annotation-processing loop run an extra round after no new source files are generated?
cards.extra: Each round scans any newly generated sources and re-invokes every processor called so far. Only after that final call does javac compile the original and generated sources, unless -proc:only was used.
cards.example:
javac -processor my.Proc App.java
# one last processor round runs after no new sources are generated,
# giving processors a chance to finish remaining work

cards.front: What is the difference between javac --release N and -target N?
cards.back: --release checks the documented API; -target sets only the version
cards.extra: --release ties source level, class-file format and the JDK's documented API together, so accidental use of newer undocumented APIs fails. -target changes only the emitted class-file version.
cards.example:
javac --release 17 MyClass.java   # --release checks the documented API
javac -target 17 MyClass.java     # -target sets only the version

cards.front: Which javac option makes compilation fail when warnings occur?
cards.extra: Useful in CI so deprecation and lint warnings cannot silently accumulate. -nowarn is the opposite knob and behaves like -Xlint:none.
cards.example:
javac -Werror -Xlint MyClass.java   # warnings make compilation fail
javac -Xlint MyClass.java           # warnings alone do not fail

cards.front: Which javac option prints supported keys for -Xlint?
cards.extra: Individual keys are enabled or disabled with -Xlint:key (prefix -key to disable); -Xlint alone enables all recommended warnings.
cards.example:
javac --help-lint   # prints supported keys for -Xlint
javac -Xlint:all MyClass.java

cards.front: What does javac -Xprefer:source change when both a source and a class file exist for an implicitly compiled type?
cards.extra: The default is -Xprefer:newer, which reads whichever of the two is newer. Source is preferred when annotation processors must see annotations with SOURCE retention.
cards.example:
javac -Xprefer:source -sourcepath src MyClass.java
# when a source and a class file both exist for an implicitly compiled type, the compiler reads the source file

cards.front: With javac -Xlint:serial, what problem is reported on a serializable class?
cards.extra: The default computed serialVersionUID depends on class details and compiler implementation, so an explicit constant avoids unexpected InvalidClassException at deserialization.
cards.example:
javac -Xlint:serial Config.java
# -Xlint:serial reports a missing serialVersionUID definition on a serializable class

cards.front: What does javac -implicit:none prevent?
cards.back: Generating class files for implicitly loaded source files
cards.extra: Implicitly loaded files are .java files the compiler pulls in for missing types. The default -implicit:class compiles them, warning when annotation processing is also active.
cards.example:
javac -implicit:none App.java
# prevents class files for implicitly loaded source files

cards.front: What does the javadoc tool produce from Java source files?
cards.extra: It parses declarations together with documentation comments. By default it documents public and protected classes, nested classes (not anonymous), interfaces, constructors, methods and fields.
cards.example:
javadoc MyClass.java          # HTML API pages generated from the Java source
javadoc -d docs MyClass.java   # same pages, written to docs/

cards.front: What is javadoc's default access level for what it documents?
cards.extra: Lower it with -package or -private; raise it with -public, which shows only public classes and members.
cards.example:
javadoc -d docs src/App.java
# default: public and protected classes and members
javadoc -private -d docs src/App.java   # everything

cards.front: Which javadoc option includes the @author text in the generated docs?
cards.extra: The tag text is otherwise dropped from output. The sibling -version option includes version text, which is likewise omitted by default.
cards.example:
javadoc -d docs -author src/App.java
# @author text is included in the generated pages

cards.front: Which javadoc option creates HTML copies of each source file with line numbers, linked from the docs?
cards.extra: It exposes private implementation details regardless of the -public/-private access options. Links are made on classes, interfaces, constructors, methods and fields.
cards.example:
javadoc -linksource -d docs MyClass.java
# HTML copies of each source with line numbers, linked from the docs

cards.front: What is the difference between javadoc -nodeprecatedlist and -nodeprecated?
cards.back: -nodeprecatedlist drops just the list page; -nodeprecated drops all of it
cards.extra: -nodeprecatedlist still generates deprecated API in the rest of the docs, only removing deprecated-list.html and its nav link. -nodeprecated does both.
cards.example:
javadoc -nodeprecatedlist src/*.java   # only the deprecation list page is dropped
javadoc -nodeprecated src/*.java       # all deprecated API documentation is dropped

cards.front: Why would you pass javadoc -notimestamp when comparing two source bases?
cards.back: It suppresses the page timestamp so diffs don't show a change on every page
cards.extra: The hidden timestamp comment includes the javadoc tool release number, so two runs on identical sources would otherwise differ on every generated page.
cards.example:
javadoc -notimestamp -d docs MyClass.java
# -notimestamp suppresses the page timestamp so diffs don't show a change on every page

cards.front: Which javadoc option makes the generated docs link to externally published javadoc?
cards.extra: The URL must point to a directory holding a package-list (or element-list for modules) file. Repeat the option for multiple external documents.
cards.example:
javadoc -d docs -link https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api src/App.java
# external API names link to that published javadoc

cards.front: When should you use javadoc -linkoffline instead of -link?
cards.back: When the external doc's list file cannot be reached over the web
cards.extra: It takes two arguments: the URL to embed in links and a location where the package-list/element-list can be found, typically locally.
cards.example:
# external doc's list file cannot be reached over the web
javadoc -linkoffline https://docs.example/api ./local-list -d docs MyClass.java

cards.front: What does the javadoc -private option document?
cards.extra: It is the most permissive of the access filters -public, -protected (default), -package and -private, which act like a visibility ladder.
cards.example:
javadoc -private -d docs MyClass.java   # all classes and members documented
javadoc -d docs MyClass.java            # default: only public/protected

cards.front: Which option generates docs for packages and all their subpackages recursively?
cards.extra: Each argument is a top-level or fully qualified package; wildcards are not allowed and -sourcepath still locates the sources. Use -exclude to carve packages out.
cards.example:
javadoc -d docs -sourcepath src -subpackages com.example
# documents the package and all its subpackages recursively

cards.front: What does the javadoc -exclude pkglist option do relative to -subpackages?
cards.extra: The exclusion wins even if an earlier or later -subpackages option would otherwise include the package, so it is the reliable way to carve out a subtree.
cards.example:
javadoc -d docs -subpackages com.example -exclude com.example.internal
# the excluded package and its subpackages stay out, even with -subpackages

cards.front: What does javadoc -nocomment generate?
cards.back: Only declarations, with the whole comment body suppressed
cards.extra: It drops the main description and all tags. Handy for reusing existing sources to produce skeleton documentation early in a project.
cards.example:
javadoc -d docs -nocomment src/App.java
# generated App.html has declarations only: no comment body or tags

cards.front: Which javadoc option builds Use pages listing what depends on each documented class or package?
cards.extra: For class C the page lists subclasses, fields of type C, methods returning C, and methods/constructors taking C. Only API usage counts, not internal implementation usage.
cards.example:
javadoc -d docs -use src/App.java
# generates a Use page for each documented class and package

cards.front: What does javadoc -splitindex do to the index?
cards.back: Splits it alphabetically, roughly one file per letter
cards.extra: Entries that start with non-alphabetic symbols go into their own extra file. It keeps very large indexes from becoming one unwieldy page.
cards.example:
javadoc -splitindex -d docs MyClass.java
# index split alphabetically, roughly one file per letter

cards.front: Which javadoc option specifies a custom doclet instead of the standard HTML one?
cards.extra: The class must be fully qualified, contain a start(Root) method, and be findable via -docletpath. A doclet defines the content and output format.
cards.example:
javadoc -doclet com.example.MyDoclet -docletpath doclets MyClass.java
# -doclet class specifies a custom doclet instead of the standard HTML one

cards.front: What is the relationship between -encoding and -docencoding in javadoc?
cards.extra: With -charset also controlling the HTML character set. If both an input and an output encoding are given, they must be the same value; with neither output option the input encoding is reused.
cards.example:
javadoc -encoding UTF-8 -docencoding ISO-8859-1 -d docs MyClass.java
# -encoding: input source; -docencoding: generated output

cards.front: What does javadoc -noqualifier all remove from the output?
cards.back: All package qualifiers from class and interface names
cards.extra: You can list specific packages instead, e.g. -noqualifier java.lang:java.io, or use wildcards such as java.*. Where a qualifier would appear it is simply dropped.
cards.example:
javadoc -noqualifier all -d docs MyClass.java
# all package qualifiers removed from class/interface names

cards.front: Is javadoc's -Xdoclint check enabled by default, and how is it turned off?
cards.extra: Groups are accessibility, html, missing, reference and syntax. The same option in javac is off by default, a notable asymmetry.
cards.example:
javadoc -Xdoclint:none -d docs MyClass.java
# -Xdoclint is enabled by default; disable it with -Xdoclint:none

cards.front: In -Xdoclint, which check group catches an item not found in @see or a bad @param name?
cards.extra: The other groups are accessibility (e.g. missing captions), html (block elements inside inline), missing (absent comments or tags) and syntax (unescaped angle brackets, ampersands).
cards.example:
javadoc -Xdoclint:reference src/*.java
# reference checks @see targets and @param names

cards.front: What does the javadoc standard doclet not do about documentation comment conformance?
cards.back: It does not validate or correct comment content
cards.extra: -Xdoclint can flag common problems, but javadoc is not a conformance checker. Output containing executable content such as JavaScript is your responsibility.
cards.example:
javadoc -d docs MyClass.java
# comment content is published as written, not validated or corrected

cards.front: What does javap do?
cards.extra: Its output depends on the options used and is printed to stdout. Without options it prints package-private, protected and public fields and methods.
cards.example:
javac App.java
javap App.class   # disassembles the class file

cards.front: With no options, which members does javap print?
cards.back: package-private, protected and public fields and methods
cards.extra: This matches the -package visibility, which is the default. Private members need -p/-private; only-public needs -public.
cards.example:
javap MyClass.class
# with no options javap prints package-private, protected and public fields and methods

cards.front: Which javap option prints the actual bytecode instructions of each method?
cards.extra: It shows the disassembled code that makes up the Java bytecodes. For extra detail on descriptors and reflection info, combine it with -s for internal type signatures.
cards.example:
javap -c App.class   # bytecode instructions for each method
javap App.class      # declarations only by default

cards.front: Which javap option shows all classes and members, including private ones?
cards.extra: The visibility ladder is -public, -protected, -package (default), and -p/-private for everything.
cards.example:
javap -p MyClass       # all classes and members, including private
javap -private MyClass  # -private is a synonym

cards.front: Which javap option prints line-number and local variable tables?
cards.extra: Those tables exist only if the class was compiled with debug info (javac -g including vars). Without them, line lookups return nothing useful.
cards.example:
javap -l MyClass.class
# -l prints line-number and local variable tables

cards.front: Which javap option prints static final constants?
cards.extra: Inlining of static final compile-time constants is why a stale constant can survive after recompiling only one class: the value is baked into callers' bytecode.
cards.example:
javap -constants MyClass.class
# -constants prints static final constants

cards.front: How does javap treat multi-release JARs when given via the class path?
cards.back: It is not multi-release aware; it shows the base entry
cards.extra: This applies to all JARs, multi-release or not. To disassemble a specific versioned class, use the URL form of the argument instead of the class-path form.
cards.example:
javap -cp app.jar com.example.App
# via the class path javap sees the base entry, not a versioned one

cards.front: Which javap option prints system information such as path, size, date and MD5 hash of the class?
cards.extra: Useful for confirming exactly which class file the tool opened when there are several on the class path. The hash also lets you compare builds.
cards.example:
javap -sysinfo App.class
# prints path, size, date and MD5 hash of the class

cards.front: Which javap option prints internal type signatures (JVMS descriptors)?
cards.extra: Descriptors like Ljava/lang/String; and (II)V appear for each member. Combine with -c when reading bytecode that calls those members.
cards.example:
javap -s MyClass.class
# -s prints internal type signatures (JVMS descriptors)

cards.front: Which javap option says which module contains the classes to disassemble?
cards.extra: Pair it with --module-path path to locate application modules, or --system jdk for system modules. The classes are then named without a path.
cards.example:
javap --module java.base java.lang.String
javap -m java.base java.lang.String   # same module selection

cards.front: How do you pass a JVM option, such as a larger heap, to the JVM that runs javap?
cards.extra: Example: -J-Xmx64m. The -J prefix is a general convention across JDK tools for forwarding options to the tool's own JVM.
cards.example:
javap MyClass             # normal javap run
javap -J-Xmx1g MyClass    # -Joption: -Xmx1g goes to javap's JVM

cards.front: What does the jdeprscan tool scan for?
cards.back: Uses of deprecated Java SE API elements
cards.extra: It is a static analysis tool over a JAR, directory, or class file. Deprecated APIs declared by third-party libraries are not reported.
cards.example:
jdeprscan --class-path . demo.MyClass
# scans for uses of deprecated Java SE API elements

cards.front: Which kinds of deprecated APIs does jdeprscan not report?
cards.extra: Only APIs deprecated by Java SE are in its database, selected by --release. Everything else relies on the compiler's own deprecation warnings.
cards.example:
jdeprscan --class-path 'libs/*' App.class
# only Java SE deprecated APIs are reported, not those from libs/*

cards.front: What must be true of the class path before jdeprscan can scan a JAR?
cards.back: All dependent classes must be present on it
cards.extra: Typically you reuse the same class path as the application run. For every class it cannot find, jdeprscan prints an error message; --class-path sets the search path.
cards.example:
jdeprscan --class-path 'lib/*' app.jar
# all classes the JAR depends on must be present on the class path

cards.front: Which jdeprscan option limits results to APIs deprecated for removal?
cards.extra: Plain deprecated APIs are excluded. It cannot be combined with a release value of 6, 7 or 8, since the for-removal marking did not exist in those releases.
cards.example:
jdeprscan App.jar                 # all deprecated APIs
jdeprscan --for-removal App.jar   # only APIs deprecated for removal

cards.front: What does jdeprscan --list do?
cards.back: Prints the set of deprecated APIs; no scanning is done
cards.extra: Because it scans nothing, you must not supply a directory, JAR, or class argument. The set depends on --release.
cards.example:
jdeprscan --list
# lists the deprecated Java SE APIs; with no class or JAR argument, nothing is scanned

cards.front: How does jdeprscan name a nested class on the command line?
cards.extra: Ordinary class names use a dot as package separator, as in java.lang.Thread. A class file path may also be named directly, e.g. build/classes/java/lang/Thread$State.class.
cards.example:
jdeprscan java.lang.Thread$State
# nested class named with $ on the command line, not with .

cards.front: In jdeprscan output, what does the method name <init> indicate?
cards.extra: Special names replace real method names: <clinit> indicates a class static initializer. All other methods appear under their plain method name, followed by argument list and return type.
cards.example:
jdeprscan --class-path . demo.MyClass
# <init> in the output denotes the constructor

cards.front: In jdeprscan output, what does a signature like (II)V mean?
cards.extra: Descriptor letters map to types: I is int, D double, V void, and Ljava/math/BigDecimal; is a reference return type. A setScale(II)V therefore takes two ints.
cards.example:
jdeprscan --class-path . App.class
# java.math.BigDecimal.setScale() -> (II)V
# (II)V: two int arguments, void return

cards.front: How far back can jdeprscan check deprecated APIs relative to the JDK you run it on?
cards.extra: For example, JDK 19 can check against earlier releases back to JDK 16. --release chooses which Java SE release supplies the deprecated-API set.
cards.example:
jdeprscan --release 17 app.jar
# jdeprscan can check deprecated APIs relative to the previous three JDK releases

cards.front: What does jdeps analyze?
cards.back: Package-level or class-level dependencies of Java class files
cards.extra: Input can be a .class file, a directory, a JAR, or a fully qualified class name. By default the dependencies are written to standard output.
cards.example:
jdeps MyClass.class                # package-level dependencies
jdeps -verbose:class MyClass.class  # class-level dependencies

cards.front: What is the default filter for dependencies in jdeps?
cards.extra: The alternative -filter:archive hides same-archive dependencies, -filter:module hides same-module ones, and -filter:none disables both package and archive filtering.
cards.example:
jdeps MyClass.class              # default -filter:package hides same-package dependencies
jdeps -filter:none MyClass.class  # show those dependencies too

cards.front: What is the difference between jdeps -verbose:package and -verbose:class?
cards.back: Package level (excluding same-package) vs class level (excluding same-archive)
cards.extra: -v/-verbose is equivalent to -verbose:class; -s/-summary prints only a dependency summary.
cards.example:
jdeps -verbose:package app.jar   # package level, skips same-package dependencies
jdeps -verbose:class app.jar     # class level, skips same-archive dependencies

cards.front: Which jdeps option restricts analysis to dependencies arising from public API signatures?
cards.extra: It looks only at public and protected members of public classes: field types, method parameter types, return types and checked exception types. Illegal internal usage is ignored.
cards.example:
jdeps -apionly MyClass.class      # only dependencies from public API signatures
jdeps MyClass.class               # all dependencies

cards.front: Which jdeps option finds dependencies on JDK internal APIs?
cards.extra: Those APIs are inaccessible under the module system, so such dependencies are a portability hazard. It cannot be combined with -p, -e, or -s.
cards.example:
jdeps --jdk-internals MyClass.class
# reports dependencies on JDK internal APIs

cards.front: Which jdeps option outputs dependencies as DOT graph files?
cards.extra: One archive-name.dot file is written per analyzed archive plus a summary.dot for the inter-archive dependencies, suitable for Graphviz.
cards.example:
jdeps --dot-output dots app.jar
# writes dots/app.jar.dot and dots/summary.dot as DOT graph files

cards.front: Which jdeps option generates a module-info.java for plain JARs?
cards.extra: Use --generate-open-module for open modules. Both cannot be combined with --dot-output or --class-path.
cards.example:
jdeps --generate-module-info generated lib.jar
# writes generated/my.module/module-info.java for the plain JAR

cards.front: Which jdeps option prints a comma-separated module list suitable for jlink --add-modules?
cards.extra: It is --list-reduced-deps with a comma-separated output, so you can paste it straight into a jlink command to build a minimal runtime image.
cards.example:
jdeps --print-module-deps app.jar
# prints a comma-separated module list suitable for jlink --add-modules

cards.front: What does jdeps --inverse report, and what must it be combined with?
cards.back: Artifacts that depend on the matching nodes — --inverse must be combined with --require, --package or --regex
cards.extra: It inverts the compile-time view: instead of what your classes use, it finds what uses them, both directly and indirectly. It prints a dependency summary.
cards.example:
jdeps --inverse --require java.sql app.jar
# --inverse reports artifacts depending on matching nodes; it needs --require, --package or --regex

cards.front: What do jdeps --check module print beyond the descriptor?
cards.back: The module dependencies, the transition-reduced graph, and unused qualified exports
cards.extra: The transition reduction hides implied read edges, and flagging unused qualified exports tells you which targeted exports could be narrowed.
cards.example:
jdeps --module-path mods --add-modules my.module --check my.module
# prints module dependencies, the transition-reduced graph, unused qualified exports

cards.front: What does jdeps -R (or -recursive) do?
cards.extra: It implies -filter:none. If -p, -e, or -f are given, only matching dependencies are analysed. --compile-time gives the compile-time equivalent.
cards.example:
jdeps -R my.jar         # -R / -recursive
jdeps -recursive my.jar  # traverses all run-time dependencies

cards.front: Which jdeps option prints which profile contains a package?
cards.extra: Profiles were the pre-module way of splitting Java SE into subsets. The profile of a dependency indicates how fundamental it is to the platform.
cards.example:
jdeps -P --package java.util app.jar
# -P (or -profile) prints which profile contains a package

cards.front: What is jlink's default module path when --module-path is not given?
cards.extra: That directory holds java.base and the other standard and JDK modules. If a module path is given but java.base cannot be resolved from it, $JAVA_HOME/jmods is appended.
cards.example:
jlink --add-modules java.base --output minimal-jre
# with no --module-path, jlink defaults to $JAVA_HOME/jmods

cards.front: What does jlink --add-modules add, given that the default root set is empty?
cards.back: The named modules as root modules, plus their transitive dependencies
cards.extra: Because jlink starts from an empty root set, you must name the application's root module or nothing useful is linked. The modules are resolved transitively from there.
cards.example:
jlink --module-path mods --add-modules my.module --output image
# my.module becomes a root module, plus its transitive dependencies

cards.front: What is the default compression level for jlink --compress?
cards.extra: Levels run from zip-0 (none) to zip-9 (maximum); zip-1 is fastest. Higher values produce smaller images at the cost of build time.
cards.example:
jlink --add-modules java.base --output default-image
jlink --add-modules java.base --compress=zip-9 --output small-image
# leaving --compress out uses the zip-6 default

cards.front: Which jlink option hides a fatal error about signed modular JARs, at the cost of not copying their signature files?
cards.extra: Signed JARs break linking because their signature files cannot survive transformation. The resulting image contains unsigned content, so consider the security implications.
cards.example:
jlink --add-modules my.module --ignore-signing-information --output image
# signed modular JARs link; their signature files are not copied

cards.front: Which jlink option creates a launcher script, e.g. myapp=com.example.app?
cards.extra: The module and main class are separated by a slash. Without it, users would have to invoke java -m module/mainclass from inside the image.
cards.example:
jlink --module-path $JAVA_HOME/jmods --add-modules com.example.app --launcher myapp=com.example.app --output myapp-image
# --launcher command=module[/mainclass] creates a launcher script

cards.front: Which jlink option strips debug symbols to shrink the image?
cards.extra: It is a plugin option. A jlink plugin can also remove native commands, exclude header files, exclude man pages, or include only selected locales.
cards.example:
jlink --strip-debug --add-modules my.module --output image
# debug symbols stripped to shrink the image

cards.front: What do jlink --no-header-files and --no-man-pages exclude?
cards.back: C header files and manual pages from the image
cards.extra: A shipped runtime rarely needs to compile native code or display man pages, so dropping both trims size with no runtime effect. jpackage passes both by default in its jlink options.
cards.example:
jlink --add-modules java.base --no-header-files --no-man-pages --output image
# image has neither C header files nor manual pages

cards.front: Which jlink option links service provider modules together with their dependencies?
cards.extra: Normally services are resolved lazily; service binding makes the image self-contained for ServiceLoader lookups. --suggest-providers lists providers implementing a service type.
cards.example:
jlink --bind-services --add-modules my.module --output image
# service provider modules are linked in with their dependencies

cards.front: Which jlink option limits the universe of observable modules?
cards.extra: The observable set becomes the transitive closure of the named modules plus the main module plus anything added via --add-modules. It is the inverse knob of --add-modules.
cards.example:
jlink --limit-modules java.base --add-modules java.logging --output minimal-jre
# --limit-modules mod[,mod...] limits the universe of observable modules

cards.front: Which jlink option lists the available plugins?
cards.extra: Plugin options such as compress, strip-debug, order-resources and include-locales are ordinary command-line options. Some need a pattern-list value.
cards.example:
jlink --list-plugins     # list plugins available in this JDK
# those plugins are enabled by their own jlink options

cards.front: In jlink options files passed with @filename, how are comments written?
cards.extra: Options can straddle one or several lines, but environment variables are not expanded in path names. This mirrors the argument-file convention of javac and other JDK tools.
cards.example:
# opts.txt: a line starting with # is a comment
--add-modules my.module
jlink @opts.txt

cards.front: What does a JMOD file contain that a JAR cannot?
cards.back: Files other than .class files: native code, config, headers, man pages
cards.extra: It aggregates class files, metadata and resources. Because of that a JMOD can hold lib/ native libraries and conf/ files that a modular JAR has no place for.
cards.example:
jmod list MyModule.jmod
# a JMOD can hold files other than .class files: native code, config, headers, man pages

cards.front: Is a JMOD file executable at run time?
cards.back: No — it is transportable but usable only at compile or link time
cards.extra: A JMOD is an input to javac's module path and to jlink. At run time you ship a modular JAR or a linked runtime image instead.
cards.example:
jmod list MyModule.jmod
# a JMOD is transportable but not executable at run time: usable only at compile or link time

cards.front: What are the jmod command's main operation modes?
cards.extra: Each mode takes the JMOD file as its argument. describe prints module details; extract unpacks everything into --dir.
cards.example:
jmod create --class-path classes app.jmod
jmod list app.jmod
jmod describe app.jmod
jmod extract --dir extracted app.jmod
# the remaining mode is hash

cards.front: What does jmod hash do?
cards.back: Records dependency hashes in the consuming modules, tying them together
cards.extra: Leaf modules are found and their hashes recorded in the modules that require them. The runtime verifies the recorded hash against the resolved module and errors out on a mismatch.
cards.example:
jmod hash --module-path mods --hash-modules '.*' mods/app.jmod
# records dependency hashes in consuming modules, tying them together

cards.front: Why does the runtime care about the hashes recorded by jmod --hash-modules?
cards.back: It verifies them at run time and errors if they don't match
cards.extra: This makes qualified exports safe: a package can be exported to exactly the named modules and no others, because a substituted module fails the hash check.
cards.example:
jmod create --class-path classes --hash-modules '.*' mb.jmod
java --module-path mods -m ma
# the runtime verifies the recorded hashes at run time and errors if they don't match

cards.front: Which jmod option specifies where extracted files are placed?
cards.extra: Used with the extract mode. On create, it is one of many options that name a source path whose contents are copied into the archive.
cards.example:
jmod extract --dir extracted MyModule.jmod
# --dir path specifies where extracted files are placed

cards.front: Which jmod option performs a dry run of hash mode?
cards.extra: It identifies the leaf modules and their required modules without recording any hash values, so you can preview what hash would tie down.
cards.example:
jmod hash --dry-run --hash-modules my.module --module-path mods mods/app.jmod
# --dry-run: hash mode performs a dry run only

cards.front: Which jmod option records the main class in module-info.class?
cards.extra: Its sibling --module-version records the module version. These let a linked image launch the module via java -m without a separate main-class argument.
cards.example:
jmod create --class-path classes --main-class com.example.App app.jmod
# --main-class records the class name in module-info.class

cards.front: Which jmod option excludes files matching patterns when copying a directory?
cards.extra: Path options otherwise copy the entire directory including subdirectories. The pattern list is comma-separated, with each element a glob, glob: regex, or @file.
cards.example:
jmod create --class-path classes --exclude '**/test/**' app.jmod
# --exclude takes patterns for files skipped while copying a directory

cards.front: Which jmod extra option hints that a module should be excluded from the default root set?
cards.extra: Its companion --warn-if-resolved takes deprecated, deprecated-for-removal, or incubating, so tools warn whenever the module is resolved.
cards.example:
jmod create --class-path classes --do-not-resolve-by-default MyModule.jmod
# --do-not-resolve-by-default hints that the module should be excluded from the default root set

cards.front: Which jmod option is required when you also specify --hash-modules?
cards.extra: Hash mode must build the module graph to know which modules require the leaf modules, so it needs the module path. Under Java Flight Recorder's config, hashing options cannot be changed after init.
cards.example:
jmod hash --hash-modules my.module --module-path mods mods/app.jmod
# --module-path (or -p) is required with --hash-modules

cards.front: What is jshell?
cards.back: A REPL that evaluates Java declarations, statements and expressions
cards.extra: It supports variable, method and class definitions, imports, and bare expressions. Each bit of entered code is called a snippet and is evaluated as you go.
cards.example:
jshell> int x = 1 + 2;          // declaration and expression
x ==> 3
jshell> System.out.println(x);  // statement
3

cards.front: What is a snippet in jshell?
cards.back: A preserved unit of entered code such as a declaration, statement or expression
cards.extra: Each snippet is evaluated immediately and receives an ID. Snippets can be dropped, edited, listed and replayed, which is why an early declaration stays available to later ones.
cards.example:
jshell> int answer = 42
jshell> answer + 1
jshell> System.out.println(answer)
# a snippet is a preserved unit of entered code: a declaration, statement or expression

cards.front: What is jshell's default feedback mode?
cards.extra: Modes are verbose, normal, concise, silent, and custom. Shortcuts for the middle two are -v, -q and -s; errors are described in every mode.
cards.example:
jshell> int answer = 42
answer ==> 42
# jshell's default feedback mode is normal

cards.front: What does jshell's -v command-line flag set?
cards.extra: It is the same as --feedback verbose. Verbose adds information about the action taken after each result and separates prompts with a blank line.
cards.example:
jshell -v                    # feedback mode set to verbose
jshell --feedback verbose    # same mode, long form

cards.front: Which jshell command lists snippets and their IDs?
cards.extra: /list -all includes startup snippets plus failed, overwritten and dropped ones. IDs starting with s are startup snippets and those starting with e are failures.
cards.example:
jshell> int x = 1;
jshell> /list
   1 : int x = 1;

cards.front: Which jshell command discards all entered snippets and restarts the session without replaying history?
cards.extra: /reload differs: it resets and then replays the history in order. /env also restarts and replays, but is aimed at changing environment settings.
cards.example:
jshell> /reset   # discards all snippets and restarts, no history replay
jshell> /list    # session is empty again

cards.front: What does the jshell /save -history option save?
cards.back: The whole session history, both snippets and commands
cards.extra: Plain /save saves only active snippets. /save -all additionally includes startup snippets and ones that failed or were overwritten.
cards.example:
jshell> int x = 1
jshell> /save -history session.jsh
# saves both snippets and commands from the whole session

cards.front: What does jshell /open file do?
cards.back: Reads the file's snippets into the current session
cards.extra: The file can be a local script or a predefined script such as DEFAULT, JAVASE, PRINTING, or TOOLING. Loading a script from an untrusted site risks executing arbitrary code.
cards.example:
jshell> /open setup.jsh
# /open file reads the file's snippets into the current session

cards.front: Which jshell command reruns the previous snippet?
cards.extra: /-n reruns the n-th previous snippet, with commands excluded from the count. Named snippets or ID ranges can be rerun with /name or /startID-endID.
cards.example:
jshell> int n = 2 * 3
jshell> /!
# reruns the previous snippet

cards.front: What does the jshell shortcut Shift+V do after entering an expression?
cards.back: Converts it into a variable declaration with the inferred type
cards.extra: Shift+M converts an expression or statement into a method declaration, and Shift+I imports the type of an unresolved identifier. All three are editing accelerators, not commands.
cards.example:
jshell> 2 + 3
jshell> int five = 2 + 3
# Shift+V converts the expression into a variable declaration with the inferred type

cards.front: Which jshell option stops the default startup scripts from running?
cards.extra: It cannot be combined with --startup, which overrides the startup script. Startup scripts also rerun on /reset, /reload, and /env.
cards.example:
jshell --no-startup   # default startup scripts are not run
jshell                # default startup scripts run

cards.front: Which option loads a script in a jshell session with inherited startup disabled for that file?
cards.extra: Startup scripts are run when jshell starts and again on /reset, /reload, and /env, so what you load at startup survives a restart of the session.
cards.example:
jshell --startup my-startup.jsl   # override the default startup script for this session
# --no-startup would disable startup scripts entirely

cards.front: How do you use jshell inside a shell pipe, feeding it standard input non-interactively?
cards.back: Pass a hyphen (-) as the load-files argument
cards.extra: The hyphen suppresses interactive I/O, so the tool reads from standard input. This makes jshell usable in pipe chains and in simple scripted experiments.
cards.example:
echo 'System.out.println(42);' | jshell -
# '-' as the load-files argument makes jshell read standard input

cards.front: What does jshell's --execution option choose?
cards.extra: Its value is an ExecutionControl spec from jdk.jshell.spi. It lets snippets run locally in-process or against a separately launched remote process.
cards.example:
jshell --execution local
# --execution takes an ExecutionControl spec naming the engine to use

cards.front: What does jshell's -C flag pass flags to?
cards.extra: Do not confuse it with -R (remote runtime) or -J (this tool's runtime). Give one instance of the option per flag or flag argument.
cards.example:
jshell -C-Xlint:deprecation
# -Cflag passes -Xlint:deprecation to jshell's compiler

cards.front: What does the jshell /set feedback command do without a mode argument?
cards.extra: Feedback modes are concise, normal, silent, verbose, or a custom mode created with /set mode. A custom mode is configured with /set prompt, /set format, and /set truncation.
cards.example:
jshell> /set feedback
# displays the current feedback mode, e.g. normal
jshell> /set feedback concise

cards.front: What does jshell /exit use as the process exit status when given an integer snippet?
cards.extra: With no argument the status is zero. If the snippet errors or does not yield an integer, an error is shown and the tool stays active.
cards.example:
jshell> /exit 7
# /exit with an integer snippet uses that integer value as the process exit status

cards.front: How do you configure a custom jshell feedback mode that shows only errors for commands?
cards.extra: -command shows info and verification feedback for commands, while -quiet shows only essential feedback such as errors. Add -retain to keep the mode across sessions.
cards.example:
jshell> /set mode quietcmds -quiet
jshell> /set feedback quietcmds
# command feedback shows only essential output such as errors

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::03 Core JDK Tools

cards.front: Which jshell option adds external libraries or JavaFX to a session's class path?
cards.extra: Since Java 9 the module form is also available with --module-path. Both can be passed at startup or changed inside a session via /env options.
cards.example:
jshell --class-path libs/dep.jar
# dep.jar is on this jshell session's class path

cards.front: Which predefined jshell script makes JDK tools like javac and jar callable as methods?
cards.extra: Loading it defines javac, jar and others, so you can compile and package without leaving the shell. tools() lists the available tools.
cards.example:
jshell
/open TOOLING
Tooling.javac("-d", "out", "Hello.java");   // JDK tools become methods

cards.front: What does calling tools() in a jshell session show?
cards.back: The list of JDK tools available via the TOOLING script
cards.extra: It must be loaded first with /open TOOLING or the --startup TOOLING option. Each tool can be invoked by name through run(String, String...).
cards.example:
jshell> /open TOOLING
jshell> tools()
# prints the list of JDK tools available via the TOOLING script

cards.front: How can jshell run an arbitrary JDK tool with arguments, without its dedicated wrapper method?
cards.extra: Example: run("javac", "-d", "out", "src/Foo.java"). The dedicated wrappers such as javac(...) are convenience methods over the same mechanism.
cards.example:
jshell> /open TOOLING
jshell> run("javac", "-version")
# run(toolName, args...) runs an arbitrary JDK tool without its dedicated wrapper method

cards.front: Which jshell command saves the current active snippets, and with which option saves the entire history?
cards.extra: The saved file is a .jsh script that can be reloaded with /open or the --startup option. -all also captures failed and overwritten snippets.
cards.example:
jshell> /save setup.jsh         # saves the current active snippets
jshell> /save -history all.jsh  # -history saves the entire history

cards.front: According to JEP 220, what can a jshell snippet not declare?
cards.extra: That is why generating a jar needs a plain source file with a package declaration. Writing snippets to a file with /save gives you a .java skeleton to add the package to.
cards.example:
jshell> package demo;   // a snippet cannot declare a package
jshell> module demo {}  // a snippet cannot declare a module

cards.front: What does src/ plus an edit session give you in a modular jshell workflow?
cards.back: A .java file whose package and module-info.java you add by hand
cards.extra: The root package directory mirrors the package tree. Then you compile with the TOOLING javac and package with jar to launch with java --module-path.
cards.example:
jshell> /edit
jshell> /save src/example/VisualJShell.java
# you then add the package declaration and module-info.java by hand

cards.front: Why is loading a remote .jsh script from jshell risky?
cards.back: Scripts contain executable code, so an untrusted source can run anything
cards.extra: There is no sandbox for loaded scripts. For scripts shared with teammates, prefer reading them into version control instead of fetching them at run time.
cards.example:
jshell https://example.com/setup.jsh
# a remote .jsh contains executable code: load only trusted sources

cards.front: Which jshell command resets state before you can rebuild a modular jar example?
cards.extra: It drops all snippets and restarts with startup scripts, but does not replay history. Use it when the previous session's classes would otherwise shadow new definitions.
cards.example:
jshell> /reset   # state is reset before rebuilding the modular jar example
jshell> /list    # no snippets remain

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::04 Monitoring and Troubleshooting

cards.front: What is JDK Flight Recorder (JFR)?
cards.back: An observability and monitoring framework built into HotSpot
cards.extra: It records events from the JVM and the application for debugging and profiling. It ships with the JDK, so no separate download or configuration step is needed.
cards.example:
String name = "JDK Flight Recorder (JFR)";
String description = "an observability and monitoring framework built into HotSpot";

cards.front: What single JVM argument enables JFR at startup?
cards.extra: It can be combined with recording options such as name, settings, duration, filename, and dumponexit, all separated by commas.
cards.example:
java -XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=rec.jfr App
# one JVM argument enables JFR at startup

cards.front: Since which JDK release can JFR be used in production without a commercial license?
cards.extra: This followed JEP 328, which contributed Flight Recorder to open source. The feature was renamed from Java Flight Recorder to JDK Flight Recorder at the same time.
cards.example:
java -XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=app.jfr App   # JDK 11 and later
# since JDK 11 JFR is free to use in production

cards.front: What is JFR's typical overhead with the default settings?
cards.extra: With profile settings it should stay under 2%. That low cost is the basis for JFR's claim that recordings can be enabled in production without harming application performance.
cards.example:
java -XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=app.jfr -jar app.jar
# with default settings JFR's typical overhead is about 1%

cards.front: What is an event in JFR?
cards.back: A self-describing element of data propagated from code execution
cards.extra: Events come from the JVM and from application code. Users configure which events are collected and can define their own events to capture application-specific data.
cards.example:
class OrderEvent extends jdk.jfr.Event {
    @jdk.jfr.Label("Order processed")
    String orderId = "A1";
    void handle() { orderId = "A2"; commit(); }
}
// a self-describing element of data emitted from code execution

cards.front: What happens when a JFR recording reaches its data-retention limit?
cards.extra: Contents go to temporary files or stay in memory, and retention is configurable. This makes JFR suitable for being always-on, much like an aircraft's flight recorder.
cards.example:
String limit = "data-retention limit";
String effect = "the oldest data is overwritten";

cards.front: Why was JFR renamed from 'Java Flight Recorder' to 'JDK Flight Recorder'?
cards.back: The rename came with open-sourcing JFR under JEP 328
cards.extra: Both names refer to the same technology. The newer name reflects that it ships with the JDK and can be used in production on JDK 11+ without a commercial licence.
cards.example:
String oldName = "Java Flight Recorder";
String newName = "JDK Flight Recorder";
// JEP 328 open-sourced JFR and renamed it

cards.front: Why is JFR described as easy to adopt but hard to master?
cards.back: It is started with one JVM flag but has many configuration layers
cards.extra: The comparison is to the board game Go. Single-arg startup sets sensible defaults, while recording options, .jfc settings files, event settings, and FlightRecorderOptions are where the depth lies.
cards.example:
java -XX:StartFlightRecording App
# one flag starts JFR; recording, .jfc, event and FlightRecorderOptions add depth

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::04 Monitoring and Troubleshooting

cards.front: When is enabling JFR at startup preferable to attaching to a running JVM?
cards.back: Startup gives the most complete picture from JVM launch onward
cards.extra: Attaching to a running JVM misses everything before the attachment, but is still useful when a process starts misbehaving and you want data before shutting it down.
cards.example:
java -XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=app.jfr -jar app.jar
# startup gives the most complete picture from JVM launch onward

cards.front: Which jcmd command starts a JFR recording on a running JVM?
cards.extra: It accepts the same recording options as -XX:StartFlightRecording, but delimited by spaces rather than commas. If no options are given, defaults are used.
cards.example:
jcmd 1234 JFR.start name=demo
# starts a JFR recording on a running JVM

cards.front: Which jcmd command writes the current JFR recording data out to a file?
cards.extra: The recording keeps running after the dump. With no filename, a name is generated from the PID and current date; name selects one recording, otherwise all are dumped.
cards.example:
jcmd 1234 JFR.dump name=demo filename=dump.jfr
# writes the current JFR recording data out to a file

cards.front: In jcmd JFR.dump, what does a begin value of -12h mean?
cards.extra: Relative times are a negative integer plus s, m, or h. Absolute times must parse as LocalTime, LocalDateTime or Instant, e.g. 2020-03-17T09:00:00.
cards.example:
jcmd 1234 JFR.dump name=demo begin=-12h filename=last12h.jfr
# begin=-12h includes data from the last 12 hours

cards.front: Why is JFR.dump path-to-gc-root=true expensive?
cards.back: Collecting GC-root paths can pause the application briefly
cards.extra: It gives you the allocation path for leaked objects, which is invaluable for memory leaks. Enable it only for an application you already suspect of leaking.
cards.example:
jcmd 21891 JFR.dump filename=leak.jfr path-to-gc-roots=true
# collecting GC-root paths can briefly pause the application

cards.front: Which jcmd JFR action requires a name argument to stop a recording?
cards.back: JFR.stop name=... — the name selects which recording to stop; without it, no recording is stopped
cards.extra: Its siblings are JFR.start, JFR.dump, JFR.configure, and JFR.check. JFR.stop discards data unless filename is supplied.
cards.example:
jcmd 1234 JFR.check            # see the active recording name
jcmd 1234 JFR.stop name=rec1   # stop the named recording

cards.front: Which jcmd command gives basic diagnostics about a JVM running JFR?
cards.extra: With no options it shows all active recordings; name narrows it and verbose=true also prints the event settings in effect, which is handy for verifying a .jfc file took effect.
cards.example:
jcmd 1234 JFR.check
# basic diagnostics about a JVM running JFR; lists active recordings

cards.front: Which tool is commonly used first to find the PID for jcmd JFR.start?
cards.extra: It lists instrumented JVMs on the local host with the main class or jar name. Any other means of getting the OS pid works too, e.g. ps or a container's process list.
cards.example:
jps
# find the lvmid first, then jcmd 21891 JFR.start

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::04 Monitoring and Troubleshooting

cards.front: How do the delimiters differ between -XX:StartFlightRecording and JFR.start when passing multiple options?
cards.extra: Both accept the identical set of recording options, so the same configuration can be written either way. Mixing delimiters is the usual cause of a rejected option.
cards.example:
java -XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=rec.jfr,settings=profile.jfc App
JFR.start filename=rec.jfr settings=profile.jfc   # jcmd uses spaces

cards.front: What are the four levels of JFR configuration?
cards.back: Recording, event, configuration (.jfc) and Flight Recorder options
cards.extra: Recording options govern overall behaviour (retention, .jfc used, dump-on-exit). Configuration settings live in .jfc files; event options govern individual events; FlightRecorderOptions tune buffers and chunking.
cards.example:
String[] levels = {"Recording", "event", "configuration (.jfc)", "Flight Recorder options"};
System.out.println(levels.length); // four levels of JFR configuration

cards.front: What is JFR's default maxsize for disk data?
cards.extra: It caps disk data when disk=true and must not be smaller than maxchunksize. Use m/M for megabytes or g/G for gigabytes.
cards.example:
java -XX:StartFlightRecording:maxsize=250m,filename=app.jfr -jar app.jar
# 250 MB is JFR's default maxsize for disk data

cards.front: What are the two predefined JFR settings files shipped in the JDK, and where are they?
cards.extra: default.jfc has low overhead and suits continuous recordings. profile.jfc collects more data at higher overhead and is meant for short diagnostic periods.
cards.example:
ls $JAVA_HOME/lib/jfr    # default.jfc and profile.jfc ship with the JDK
# JAVA_HOME/bin/jfr configures event settings

cards.front: What does the dumponexit recording option do, and what is its default?
cards.back: Dumps the recording when the JVM shuts down; default is false
cards.extra: If enabled without a filename, a file is written to the process's start directory with a generated name containing the PID, recording ID and timestamp.
cards.example:
boolean dumponexit = false;
// when true, dumps the recording when the JVM shuts down; default false

cards.front: What does the maxage recording option control?
cards.back: The maximum age of disk data kept for the recording
cards.extra: It is valid only when disk=true and defaults to 0s (unlimited). Times take an s, m, h or d suffix, e.g. 30s.
cards.example:
java -XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=app.jfr,maxage=1h App
# maxage: maximum age of disk data kept for the recording

cards.front: What does the settings recording option point to?
cards.back: The path of an event settings file of type .jfc
cards.extra: The .jfc also holds controls that JDK Mission Control uses. As of JDK 19 the recommended way to build settings files is the jfr configure utility.
cards.example:
java -XX:StartFlightRecording:settings=/path/custom.jfc,filename=app.jfr -jar app.jar
# settings points to an event settings file of type .jfc

cards.front: Which JFR event option governs how long an event may run before it is recorded?
cards.extra: Its value is a duration, defaulting to 0. By contrast period sets the minimum time between recordings of the same periodic event.
cards.example:
String option = "threshold";
String meaning = "how long an event may run before it is recorded";

cards.front: What is the default value of the JFR event option stackTrace?
cards.extra: Stack traces are collected for every event unless disabled. They cost memory in the buffers, so busy events are sometimes recorded without them, but they are what makes recordings diagnostic.
cards.example:
class TraceEvent extends jdk.jfr.Event {
    void sample() { commit(); }
}
// the JFR stackTrace event option defaults to true

cards.front: What does the -XX:FlightRecorderOptions maxchunksize default to, and what is its minimum?
cards.extra: Chunks are the unit written to disk; a chunk holds all data needed to parse it. memorysize (default 10 MB) sizes the buffers, and repository sets the temp dir.
cards.example:
java -XX:FlightRecorderOptions:maxchunksize=12M App   # default
java -XX:FlightRecorderOptions:maxchunksize=1M App    # minimum allowed

cards.front: What is the default JFR stackdepth, and why not raise it casually?
cards.back: 64 frames; deeper stacks can cost significant overhead
cards.extra: The maximum is 2048. Raising it slows the app and enlarges recordings, so tune it only when a specific 65-deep frame trend is what you need to see.
cards.example:
java -XX:FlightRecorderOptions:stackdepth=64 App
# default 64 frames; deeper stacks can create significant overhead

cards.front: What does -XX:FlightRecorderOptions retransform=true enable?
cards.extra: It is the default; with false, instrumentation is instead added when event classes load. Disabling retransform matters when another agent relies on class shapes.
cards.example:
java -XX:FlightRecorderOptions:retransform=true App
# event classes are retransformed using JVMTI

cards.front: What does the delay recording option control?
cards.back: The wait between application launch and recording start
cards.extra: Default is 0. It takes s, m, h, or d, e.g. 10m, so a scheduled recording can skip warm-up or catch a later steady-state window.
cards.example:
java -XX:StartFlightRecording:delay=10m,filename=app.jfr -jar app.jar
# delay is the wait between application launch and recording start

cards.front: Since which JDK release can event options be set directly on the command line rather than in a .jfc file?
cards.extra: They work on -XX:StartFlightRecording, JFR.start, and JFR.configure. Precedence is command line over .jfc file over annotations in the event class.
cards.example:
java -XX:StartFlightRecording:jdk.JavaMonitorWait#enabled=true,filename=rec.jfr App
# since JDK 17 event options work on the command line and override .jfc

cards.front: What is the jfr command for?
cards.back: Parsing, summarising and printing .jfr recording files
cards.extra: It filters and converts binary recordings into human-readable output, and supports merging and splitting. It operates on files, not on live JVMs.
cards.example:
jfr summary rec.jfr   # summarise a .jfr recording
jfr print rec.jfr      # print its contents as text

cards.front: Which jfr subcommand prints events in a filterable human-readable form?
cards.extra: Options include --events and --categories filters, --stack-depth, and machine-readable --json or --xml output.
cards.example:
jfr print --events CPULoad recording.jfr
# human-readable events, filterable with --events and --categories

cards.front: What is the default number of stack-trace frames shown by jfr print?
cards.extra: Change it with --stack-depth. Truncation is why a promising stack sometimes stops just short of the frame you want to see.
cards.example:
jfr print rec.jfr                     # 5 stack-trace frames by default
jfr print --stack-depth 10 rec.jfr    # explicit frame count

cards.front: In jfr print, how do the event and category filters combine?
cards.back: As a union of the two selections
cards.extra: Matching is on symbolic event names (@Name) and categories (@Category). With no filter all events print, and multiple names in one filter are comma-separated.
cards.example:
jfr print --categories GC --events CPULoad recording.jfr
# both filters apply: the selected events are the union

cards.front: Which jfr subcommand displays aggregated event data rather than raw events?
cards.extra: Named views summarise a recording into tables; all-views shows every view and all-events shows every event. --verbose reveals the query behind the view.
cards.example:
jfr view events-by-count recording.jfr
# displays aggregated event data rather than raw events

cards.front: Which jfr subcommand prints statistics such as event counts and disk usage?
cards.extra: It is the quickest way to judge whether an .jfc setting was appropriate, since a recording that is all one event type usually signals a mis-tuning.
cards.example:
jfr summary recording.jfr
# prints statistics such as event counts and disk usage

cards.front: Which jfr subcommand removes events from a recording, e.g. before sharing it?
cards.extra: It filters by event, category, and thread, which lets you strip sensitive payload. Without an output file the result is written beside the input with -scrubbed appended.
cards.example:
jfr scrub recording.jfr
# removes events from a recording, e.g. before sharing it

cards.front: Which jfr subcommand turns chunk files back into a recording?
cards.extra: Chunks survive a JVM crash on disk, so assembling recovers a usable recording. Chunks are concatenated chronologically and unfinished .part files are skipped.
cards.example:
jfr assemble repository recording.jfr
# chunk files become a flight recording file

cards.front: Why would you run jfr disassemble on a recording?
cards.back: To repair a broken file by dropping the faulty chunk, or split a huge file
cards.extra: Output goes to --output (default current directory) as myfile_1.jfr, myfile_2.jfr, zero-padded when there are more than 99 parts.
cards.example:
jfr disassemble --output parts recording.jfr
# repairs a broken file by dropping the faulty chunk, or splits a huge file

cards.front: What is the default number of chunks per output file for jfr disassemble?
cards.extra: Set it with --max-chunks, or cap bytes with --max-size. A chunk's size varies but is typically around 15 MB.
cards.example:
jfr disassemble recording.jfr
# default: at most 5 chunks per output file

cards.front: Which jfr subcommand builds a .jfc settings file non-interactively?
cards.extra: Without --output it writes custom.jfc; --input none starts from an empty configuration, and prefixing an event name with + adds an event setting.
cards.example:
jfr configure --output custom.jfc --verbose
# builds a .jfc settings file without --interactive

cards.front: Which jfr subcommand shows event names, categories and field layout stored in a recording?
cards.extra: It reads the metadata embedded in the .jfr file rather than the event payload, which is what you need before writing jfr print --events or --categories filters.
cards.example:
jfr metadata rec.jfr   # event names, categories and field layout in the recording
# jfr summary rec.jfr shows statistics instead

cards.front: Which jfr subcommand lists the version string of the tool itself, not of a recording?
cards.extra: Per-subcommand help comes from jfr --help subcommand. Because jfr ships with the JDK, this version identifies the JDK whose event metadata you are reading.
cards.example:
jfr --version
jfr version
# prints the version string of the jfr tool itself, not of a recording

cards.front: How does a jdk.jfr.Percentage annotated field with value 0.52 appear in jfr print?
cards.extra: Fields are formatted according to their declared content types, not raw values. So percentages, durations and memory sizes are already humanised unless --json or --xml is used.
cards.example:
class LoadEvent extends jdk.jfr.Event {
    @jdk.jfr.Percentage
    double used = 0.52;
    void sample() { commit(); }
}
// jfr print shows used as 52%

cards.front: How do you get machine-readable output from jfr print?
cards.extra: The default is human-readable text. JSON and XML are the supported formats for post-processing with your own scripts, and their field values are not pre-formatted.
cards.example:
jfr print --json recording.jfr
jfr print --xml recording.jfr
# machine-readable output

cards.front: What does jfr view --truncate beginning change?
cards.back: Overlong table cells keep their start instead of their end
cards.extra: The default is end, which keeps the tail of a value. --cell-height caps rows per cell and --width sets the total character width.
cards.example:
jfr view --truncate beginning events-by-count recording.jfr
# overlong table cells keep their start instead of their end

cards.front: In jfr configure, what does prefixing an event name with + do?
cards.back: Adds a new event setting to the .jfc file
cards.extra: The syntax is event#setting=value, where # is the setting name. Existing settings are modified by naming them without the + prefix.
cards.example:
jfr configure --input default.jfc --output custom.jfc '+MyEvent#enabled=true'
# a + prefix adds a new event setting to the .jfc file

cards.front: Which jfr configure option makes the tool ask questions to build the configuration?
cards.extra: It walks through the choices rather than requiring you to know option names. --verbose then prints the resulting modified settings so you can review them.
cards.example:
jfr configure --interactive
# asks questions to build the configuration; --verbose shows the settings

cards.front: What does jfr scrub do when no output file is given?
cards.back: Writes the result next to the input with -scrubbed appended
cards.extra: This matters in pipelines that expect the input file to be untouched. Specify an explicit output path when the tool will later read the original again.
cards.example:
jfr scrub recording.jfr
# writes recording-scrubbed.jfr next to the input when no output is given

cards.front: In jfr scrub, what happens when an event matches both an include and an exclude filter?
cards.back: Filters are applied in the order specified
cards.extra: So a later include can re-add what an earlier exclude removed, or vice versa. Include and exclude filters exist for events, categories, and threads alike.
cards.example:
jfr scrub --exclude-events jdk.JavaMonitorWait --include-events jdk.ThreadSleep recording.jfr out.jfr
# multiple filters are applied in the order specified

cards.front: What does a jfr disassemble chunk file of myfile_001.jfr imply about the recording?
cards.extra: File names are zero-padded to preserve chronological ordering when concatenated, so a fixed width signals a large count. Directories and glob expansion sort correctly because of it.
cards.example:
jfr disassemble --output parts recording.jfr
ls parts/myfile_001.jfr
# zero-padded _001 implies more than 100 chunks in the recording

cards.front: Why does jfr assemble exclude .part chunk files?
cards.back: They are unfinished chunks, so they cannot be parsed reliably
cards.extra: Chunks are written progressively; the .part suffix marks the one that was in flight at the time of a crash. Its data is incomplete and would corrupt the assembly.
cards.example:
jfr assemble parts recording.jfr
# .part chunks are unfinished, so they cannot be parsed reliably

cards.front: What is jconsole?
cards.back: A graphical console to monitor and manage Java applications
cards.extra: It connects to a local or remote JVM using the JMX management agent and shows live threads, memory, classes, and JVM internals. It needs a GUI display.
cards.example:
jconsole 1234
# opens a graphical console to monitor and manage the Java application

cards.front: What is the default update interval for jconsole?
cards.extra: Change it with -interval n. On a graph, a shorter interval shows burstier detail; a longer one smooths the trace but hides short spikes.
cards.example:
jconsole 21891
# default update interval is 4 seconds (-interval n changes it)

cards.front: What forms can jconsole's connection argument take?
cards.extra: A pid requires the target JVM to run under the same user ID. A host:port must match com.sun.management.jmxremote.port set when the JVM started.
cards.example:
jconsole 21891                       # pid
jconsole localhost:9010              # host:port
jconsole service:jmx:rmi:///jndi/rmi://localhost:9999/jmxrmi   # JMX URL

cards.front: Why would jconsole fail to attach using a pid?
cards.back: The target JVM runs under a different user ID
cards.extra: PID attachment uses the local attach mechanism, which enforces same-user access. For a different account, start the target with a JMX remote port and connect with host:port.
cards.example:
jconsole 1234                  # requires the same user ID as the target JVM
# a JVM under a different user ID cannot be attached to by pid

cards.front: What does the jconsole -notile option change?
cards.back: It stops tiling the windows of two or more connections
cards.extra: By default multiple connection windows are arranged side by side inside a single window. Untiling lets you place them yourself, e.g. across separate displays.
cards.example:
jconsole -notile 1234 remote.example.org:9010   # two connections, windows not tiled
# without -notile the windows would be tiled

cards.front: Which jconsole option tells it where to look for plug-ins?
cards.extra: Each directory in that path needs a provider-configuration file at META-INF/services/com.sun.tools.jconsole.JConsolePlugin naming the implementing class.
cards.example:
jconsole -pluginpath /path/to/plugins 1234
# -pluginpath tells jconsole where to look for plug-ins

cards.front: What does jps list?
cards.back: Instrumented Java HotSpot JVMs on the target system
cards.extra: For each it reports the lvmid plus, by default, the short form of the main class or jar name. It only sees JVMs the running user has access to.
cards.example:
jps
# lists instrumented Java HotSpot JVMs on the target system

cards.front: What is an lvmid?
cards.back: The local JVM identifier, usually the OS pid but not required to be
cards.extra: It is the lvmid component of a vmid in tools like jstat. Because it is only typically the OS pid, code should not assume they are interchangeable.
cards.example:
jps -q        # prints only local JVM identifiers (lvmids)
# an lvmid is usually the OS pid, but need not be

cards.front: Which jps option shows arguments passed to the main method?
cards.extra: Output may be null for embedded JVMs. Do not confuse it with -v, which shows arguments the JVM itself received.
cards.example:
jps -m
# shows arguments passed to the main method

cards.front: What is the difference between jps -l and jps -m?
cards.back: -l shows the full class/jar name; -m shows main arguments
cards.extra: The other selectors are -v for JVM arguments and -q for only the identifiers. Any combination of -mlvV is accepted.
cards.example:
jps -l      # full class name or jar name
jps -m      # arguments passed to the main method

cards.front: Which jps option suppresses the class name and main arguments, leaving only identifiers?
cards.extra: Both produce a bare list of local JVM identifiers, convenient for shell loops. Neither adds information; they remove it, which makes parsing less fragile.
cards.example:
jps -q    # only lvmids: no class name, JAR name or main args
jps -V    # same suppression

cards.front: When jps hostid targets a remote host, what must be running on that host?
cards.extra: The remote lookup uses the RMI protocol via the jstatd server, on the default rmiregistry port 1099 unless specified. Local listing needs nothing extra.
cards.example:
jps remote.example.org   # hostid queries a remote host
# a jstatd process must be running on that host

cards.front: Why does jps sometimes print Unknown for the class name?
cards.back: The JVM was started with a custom launcher
cards.extra: The Java launcher supplies the main class and arguments that jps reports. Without it, those values are unavailable and Unknown replaces each of them.
cards.example:
jps          # a JVM started with a custom launcher prints Unknown
# its class/JAR name and main args are not available to jps

cards.front: Should you parse jps output in scripts?
cards.back: No — the format may change in future releases
cards.extra: The same caution applies to jstat. Tokenisation also breaks when an argument contains embedded whitespace, so prefer the JVM APIs for programmatic use.
cards.example:
jps -l
# do not parse the output in scripts; the format may change in future releases
