cards.front: What does jstat display?
cards.back: Performance statistics for an instrumented HotSpot JVM
cards.extra: It targets a JVM by vmid and supports two option kinds: general options (help, version) and output options that choose which statistics are shown.
cards.example:
jstat -gcutil 21891 250 7
# performance statistics for an instrumented HotSpot JVM

cards.front: What does jstat -gcutil show?
cards.extra: It reports per-space utilisation percentages (E, O, S0, S1) plus counts and times of young and full collections. It is the usual first look at GC health.
cards.example:
jstat -gcutil 1234 1000   # summary of garbage collection statistics every 1000 ms
# gcutil prints utilisation percentages

cards.front: What is the difference between jstat -gcutil and jstat -gccause?
cards.back: -gccause adds the cause of the last and current GC events
cards.extra: Both otherwise print the same summary. The added cause columns are what tell you whether a full GC was triggered by allocation failure, System.gc, or an ergonomics decision.
cards.example:
jstat -gcutil 1234
jstat -gccause 1234
# -gccause adds the cause of the last and current GC events

cards.front: What does jstat -gcnew display?
cards.extra: Its columns include survivor and eden usage plus the tenuring threshold (TT) and desired survivor size (DSS). -gcnewcapacity complements it with the space sizes.
cards.example:
jstat -gcnew 1234
# displays statistics about the new generation

cards.front: In jstat output, which option shows old generation and metaspace behaviour?
cards.extra: It covers both old-generation behaviour and metaspace statistics. For old-generation sizes only, -gcoldcapacity; for metaspace sizes, -gcmetacapacity.
cards.example:
jstat -gcold 1234
# shows old generation and metaspace behaviour

cards.front: What does jstat -h n do?
cards.back: Prints the column header every n samples
cards.extra: Without it the header appears once at the top and scrolls away during a long sample run. The default value 0 means header only on the first line.
cards.example:
jstat -gcutil -h 5 1234 1000    # header every 5 samples
# the default prints the header only on the first row

cards.front: What does jstat -t add to its output?
cards.back: A Timestamp column of seconds since the JVM started
cards.extra: Because the timestamp measures from JVM start rather than wall-clock time, aligning jstat samples with an external log requires adding the JVM's own start time.
cards.example:
jstat -gcutil -t 21891 1000 3
# -t adds a Timestamp column: seconds since the JVM started

cards.front: What are jstat's default units for the interval argument?
cards.extra: Append s for seconds. count defaults to infinity, so jstat keeps sampling until the JVM or jstat exits; give a positive integer to bound the run.
cards.example:
jstat -gcutil 1234      # interval defaults to milliseconds
jstat -gcutil 1234 250   # sample every 250 milliseconds

cards.front: What does jstat -J-Xms48m do?
cards.back: Passes -Xms48m to the jstat tool's own JVM
cards.extra: The -J prefix never reaches the monitored target. To affect the target, you would have to pass options at its own launch, not through jstat.
cards.example:
jstat -J-Xms48m -gcutil 1234   # -Xms48m goes to jstat's own JVM
# the target JVM's heap settings are unchanged

cards.front: What does the jstat -options general option list?
cards.back: The available stat options for that platform installation
cards.extra: It is the authoritative list for the local JVM, which matters because options may be changed or removed between releases. Using it with another option is not allowed.
cards.example:
jstat -options    # stat options available for this platform installation
# use one of the listed options as jstat -gcutil

cards.front: In jstat output for -gcnew, what does a falling tenuring threshold (TT) indicate?
cards.back: Survivors were promoted early because survivor space overflowed
cards.extra: When survivor usage exceeds the desired survivor size (DSS), objects move to the old generation and TT is lowered. A subsequent light collection can push TT back up.
cards.example:
jstat -gcnew 1234
# a falling tenuring threshold (TT) means survivors were promoted early because survivor space overflowed

cards.front: In a jstat vmid, what is the only required component?
cards.extra: Protocol, hostname, port, and servername are optional. Omitting both protocol and hostname selects a platform-optimised local protocol; naming a host without a protocol defaults to RMI.
cards.example:
jstat -gcutil 21891 250 7
# 21891 is the lvmid: the only required part of a vmid

cards.front: What is the jstatd command?
cards.back: An RMI server that monitors instrumented JVM creation and termination
cards.extra: It gives remote monitoring tools such as jstat and jps a way to attach to JVMs on the host and read their instrumentation.
cards.example:
jstatd
# RMI server monitoring instrumented JVM creation and termination

cards.front: What port does jstatd use by default for the RMI registry?
cards.extra: Set a different port with -p port. If no registry exists at that port, jstatd starts one internally unless -nr is given.
cards.example:
jstatd
# the RMI registry defaults to port 1099

cards.front: What does jstatd -nr do?
cards.back: Stops it from creating an internal RMI registry
cards.extra: It is used when an external registry should already be running. If none is found, jstatd reports an error instead of silently binding its own.
cards.example:
jstatd -nr      # do not create an internal RMI registry
# an external rmiregistry must already be running

cards.front: What does jstatd -r rmiport set?
cards.back: The port the RMI connector binds to
cards.extra: This is distinct from the registry port set by -p. If omitted, a random available port is used, which can defeat firewall rules unless both are pinned.
cards.example:
jstatd -p 1099 -r 2021
# -r sets the port the RMI connector binds to

cards.front: What is the default name bound for jstatd's remote RMI object, and which option changes it?
cards.extra: Run multiple jstatd servers on one host and each needs a unique name. Clients must then include that name in their hostid and vmid strings.
cards.example:
jstatd                  # binds the remote RMI object as JStatRemoteHost
jstatd -n MyStatServer  # -n rminame changes that bound name

cards.front: Does jstatd authenticate remote clients?
cards.extra: Anyone on the network who can reach it acquires the instrumentation of every JVM it has permission to read. Treat it as a local-tool-only option unless the network is trusted.
cards.example:
jstatd -p 1099
# no authentication: any reachable client sees the JVMs jstatd can monitor

cards.front: Which permission constraint applies to what jstatd can monitor?
cards.back: Only JVMs it can natively access, so it must run under the same user as them
cards.extra: A process with root credentials can attach to anything, but that greatly widens exposure. Running as root for monitoring is a security tripwire, not a convenience.
cards.example:
String scope = "only JVMs it can natively access";
String requirement = "jstatd must run under the same user as them";

cards.front: Why does running without a security manager make jstatd require a policy file?
cards.back: It installs an RMISecurityPolicy instance by default
cards.extra: The policy file must follow the standard policy syntax. If your security needs exceed what a policy file can express, the safest move is not to run jstatd at all.
cards.example:
String policy = "without a security manager, jstatd installs an RMISecurityPolicy by default";
String effect = "so a policy file is required";

cards.front: Which JVMs does jps fail to list when using jstatd?
cards.extra: Container PID namespaces hide those processes from the host-side instrumented listing. Use ps inside the container or expose the container's own port instead.
cards.example:
jstatd -p 1099 &
jps remote.host   # JVMs inside docker containers are not listed

cards.front: Why not write against the interface exported by jstatd?
cards.back: It is proprietary and guaranteed to change
cards.extra: There is no compatibility promise, so code depending on it will break on a future JDK. Use the jstat and jps command-line tools, or JMX, for automation.
cards.example:
String api = "interface exported by jstatd";
String reason = "proprietary and guaranteed to change";

cards.front: What does the jcmd utility do?
cards.back: Sends diagnostic command requests to a running JVM
cards.extra: It must run on the same machine as the JVM and under the same effective user and group. Each diagnostic command has its own syntax and arguments.
cards.example:
jcmd 21891 VM.flags
# sends a diagnostic command request to the running JVM

cards.front: What does jcmd with no arguments do?
cards.back: Lists running JVMs — the same as jcmd -l
cards.extra: The listing shows the process identifier, main class, and launch arguments, but excludes JVMs running in separate docker processes.
cards.example:
jcmd
# same as jcmd -l: lists running JVMs with pid, main class and arguments

cards.front: How do you discover the available diagnostic commands for a given JVM?
cards.extra: Adding the command name, as in jcmd pid help VM.flags, shows that command's description, syntax and arguments. Guessing command names and arguments is never necessary.
cards.example:
jcmd 1234 help
jcmd 1234 help VM.flags
# discovers the diagnostic commands available for that JVM

cards.front: What does jcmd 0 command do?
cards.back: Sends the command to all Java processes
cards.extra: The pid 0 is the broadcast selector. You can equivalently pass a main-class name, matched partially or fully, to target every JVM started from that class.
cards.example:
jcmd 0 VM.flags
# pid 0 sends the command to all Java processes

cards.front: Which command produces a HPROF heap dump from a running JVM?
cards.extra: It is high impact and requests a full GC unless -all is given. For live-only content the default is preferable; use -all when you need unreachable objects.
cards.example:
jcmd 1234 GC.heap_dump heap.hprof
# produces an HPROF heap dump from a running JVM

cards.front: Which jcmd command prints a histogram of heap classes by instance count?
cards.extra: It is high impact because it walks the heap. -all includes unreachable objects; default counts only reachable ones, which is usually what you want for a leak hunt.
cards.example:
jcmd 1234 GC.class_histogram   # histogram of heap classes by instance count
# pass -all to include unreachable objects

cards.front: Which jcmd command prints all thread stack traces?
cards.extra: The option -l also prints java.util.concurrent locks. This is the in-flight equivalent of the standalone jstack tool.
cards.example:
jcmd 1234 Thread.print    # print all thread stack traces
# jcmd 0 Thread.print targets every Java process

cards.front: Which jcmd command prints the VM flags and their current values?
cards.extra: VM.flags -all prints every flag the VM supports. This is the authoritative answer to 'what is this JVM actually configured with', including defaults.
cards.example:
jcmd 1234 VM.flags
# prints the VM flags and their current values

cards.front: Which jcmd command changes a VM flag on a running JVM?
cards.extra: Only flags declared as manageable can be changed at run time. Others are locked once the JVM starts, and the command will refuse them.
cards.example:
jcmd 1234 VM.set_flag HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError true
# changes a VM flag on the running JVM

cards.front: Which jcmd command reports native memory usage by subsystem?
cards.extra: It needs the JVM launched with NMT enabled. baseline snapshots current usage and summary.diff reports growth against it, which pinpoints the leaking subsystem.
cards.example:
jcmd 1234 VM.native_memory summary
# reports native memory usage by subsystem

cards.front: What does jcmd VM.native_memory baseline accomplish for a later diff?
cards.back: Records current usage as a reference point
cards.extra: The subsequent detail.diff then shows allocation activity since that baseline at each call site. Without a baseline, the diff commands have nothing to compare against.
cards.example:
jcmd 1234 VM.native_memory baseline      # record current usage as a reference point
jcmd 1234 VM.native_memory summary.diff   # compare later against that baseline

cards.front: Which jcmd command lists all loaded classes in hierarchy form?
cards.extra: Each class is followed by its ClassLoaderData pointer, or null for the bootstrap loader. -s shows subclasses, and -i includes inherited interfaces.
cards.example:
jcmd 21891 VM.class_hierarchy
# lists all loaded classes in hierarchy form

cards.front: Which jcmd command rotates the JVM's unified-logging outputs?
cards.extra: VM.log list shows the current configuration. Setting disable=true turns all logging off and clears the configuration, so use it deliberately.
cards.example:
jcmd 1234 VM.log rotate
# rotates the JVM's unified-logging outputs

cards.front: Which jcmd command reports the JVM's uptime?
cards.extra: -date prefixes the output with the current date. Since jstat -t timestamps are relative to JVM start, uptime lets you convert them to wall-clock time.
cards.example:
jcmd 1234 VM.uptime
# VM.uptime reports the JVM's uptime; VM.uptime -date adds the date

cards.front: Which jcmd command prints all methods ever touched during this JVM's lifetime?
cards.extra: Useful for finding dead code that still gets linked, and for auditing what a loaded agent actually invoked. It is not the same as the compiled-method list.
cards.example:
jcmd 1234 VM.print_touched_methods
# prints all methods ever touched during this JVM's lifetime

cards.front: Which jcmd command dumps the JVM's string table?
cards.extra: -verbose also dumps the content of every string, which can be huge and may expose user data. The parallel command for interned symbols is VM.symboltable.
cards.example:
jcmd 1234 VM.stringtable
# dumps the JVM's string table

cards.front: Which jcmd command shows the command line used to start the VM?
cards.extra: It reports the launch line recorded in ProcessHandle terms, which may differ in presentation from what ps shows. Compare with VM.system_properties for resolved paths.
cards.example:
jcmd 1234 VM.command_line
# shows the command line used to start the VM

cards.front: What does jcmd VM.version print?
cards.extra: VM.info is the fuller report covering environment and status. Neither is the same as asking a running app what its Java java.version property says.
cards.example:
jcmd 1234 VM.version
# prints the JVM version information

cards.front: Why does jcmd fail when run by a different user than the target JVM?
cards.back: It requires the same effective user and group as the JVM's launch
cards.extra: The attach mechanism checks credentials at the OS level. Parent process identity, groups, and container boundaries all affect whether the attach is permitted.
cards.example:
jcmd 1234 VM.version
# requires the same effective user and group as the JVM's launch, or it fails

cards.front: In jcmd, how are command options written when the command defines them?
cards.extra: Flags given as key are usually Boolean options. This differs from the positional arguments some commands take, such as a heap-dump filename.
cards.example:
jcmd 1234 JFR.start name=demo settings=profile
jcmd 1234 VM.uptime -date
# command options use key or key=value syntax

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::04 Monitoring and Troubleshooting

cards.front: What is jdb?
cards.back: A simple command-line debugger for Java classes
cards.extra: It demonstrates the Java Platform Debugger Architecture and can debug a local or remote JVM. Its command set mirrors the textbook debugger workflow and suits automation.
cards.example:
jdb App   # simple command-line debugger for Java classes
# it inspects and debugs Java classes from the command line

cards.front: How do you start jdb so it launches the application itself?
cards.back: Substitute jdb for java on the command line
cards.extra: It starts a second JVM, loads the class, and stops before the first instruction of the main class. No separate debug-server setup is needed for this mode.
cards.example:
javac App.java
jdb App    # jdb in place of java launches the application itself

cards.front: Which kind of JVM options must a target JVM be started with so jdb can attach?
cards.back: The in-process debugging libraries, specifying a connection
cards.extra: Often written as -agentlib:jdwp=... with an address. Without them, the JVM accepts no debugger connection at all.
cards.example:
String tool = "jdb";
String requirement = "target JVM started with in-process debugging libraries, specifying a connection";

cards.front: Which jdb command sets a breakpoint at a specific line?
cards.extra: It resolves to the first instruction for line 22 of the source file containing MyClass. stop in java.lang.String.length instead breaks at a method's first instruction.
cards.example:
jdb MyClass
> stop at MyClass:22
# sets a breakpoint at line 22

cards.front: What is required when setting a breakpoint on an overloaded method?
cards.extra: For example stop in MyClass.myMethod(int,java.lang.String). Without types, jdb cannot tell which overload you mean, so it cannot set the breakpoint.
cards.example:
stop in MyClass.myMethod(int,java.lang.String)   # jdb: argument types pick the overload
stop in MyClass.myMethod()                       # the no-argument overload

cards.front: Which jdb command removes a breakpoint?
cards.extra: Running clear or stop with no argument lists the currently set breakpoints. Resuming execution after a stop uses cont.
cards.example:
jdb MyClass
> clear MyClass:45
# removes the breakpoint at line 45

cards.front: What is the difference between jdb step and jdb next?
cards.back: step follows calls; next stays in the current frame
cards.extra: Step advances to the next line whether it is in this frame or a called method. Next advances to the next line in the same frame, treating calls as a single step.
cards.example:
step   # jdb: follows calls into the called method
next   # stays in the current stack frame

cards.front: When a thread hits an uncaught exception under jdb, what happens instead of the JVM exiting?
cards.back: Control returns to jdb at the throw
cards.extra: Without a debugger the JVM usually prints a trace and exits. At the break, you can inspect variables and the stack to find the cause before it unwinds.
cards.example:
jdb App
main[1] run
# on an uncaught exception control returns to jdb at the throw

cards.front: Which jdb command makes it stop whenever a given exception is thrown?
cards.extra: Any instance of the class or a subclass stops execution where it is thrown. ignore reverses the effect for the debugger, not for the application.
cards.example:
jdb App
main[1] catch java.io.FileNotFoundException
# stops whenever that exception is thrown

cards.front: What does jdb ignore actually do?
cards.back: Reverts a catch, making the debugger ignore that exception
cards.extra: It does not change exception handling in the application. If the app catches and swallows an exception, jdb still sees the throw unless catch tells it to stop there.
cards.example:
jdb MyClass
> catch java.io.IOException
> ignore java.io.IOException
# ignore reverts the catch; the debugger ignores that exception

cards.front: What does jdb -launch change about startup?
cards.back: It starts the application immediately, removing the need for run
cards.extra: The app then stops just before the initial class is loaded, giving you a chance to set breakpoints first. This avoids missing early execution.
cards.example:
jdb -launch App    # start the application immediately at jdb startup
# no run command is needed; use cont after setting breakpoints

cards.front: Which jdb option waits for a running JVM to connect at any available address?
cards.extra: The opposite direction is -attach address, where jdb connects out to a JVM. -listen address waits on one specific address.
cards.example:
jdb -listenany    # wait for a running JVM to connect at any available address
# the target JVM attaches to the address jdb reports

cards.front: Which jdb option lists the connectors available in the JVM?
cards.extra: Connector names are then used with -connect connector-name:name1=value1,.... This is how you pick a non-default transport without guessing its name.
cards.example:
jdb -listconnectors
# lists the connectors available in the JVM

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::04 Monitoring and Troubleshooting

cards.front: What is jhsdb used for?
cards.back: Postmortem analysis of a core dump from a crashed JVM
cards.extra: It launches a debugger against a core file (or attaches to a process) and exposes modes mirroring the jstack, jmap, jinfo and jsnap tools.
cards.example:
jhsdb jstack --exe /path/to/java --core core.dump
# postmortem analysis of a core dump from a crashed JVM

cards.front: What happens if you attach jhsdb to a live process?
cards.back: The process hangs and probably crashes when the debugger detaches
cards.extra: jhsdb suspends the target while it works, so it is not a safe live diagnostic. For a running JVM use jcmd, jstack, or jmap instead.
cards.example:
jhsdb jstack --pid 1234
# attaching to a live process hangs it and probably crashes it when the debugger detaches

cards.front: What is required to analyze a core dump with jhsdb instead of a pid?
cards.extra: Both must be supplied together. Alternatively a [server-id@]debugd-host can be used. Any one of these three forms satisfies the requirement.
cards.example:
jhsdb jstack --exe /path/to/java --core /path/to/core
# core analysis requires the Java executable and the core file

cards.front: Which jhsdb mode starts an interactive command-line debugger?
cards.extra: It is the text-session counterpart of the GUI mode hssdb (hsdb). The others are batch-style modes that mimic familiar JDK tools.
cards.example:
jhsdb clhsdb
# starts the interactive command-line debugger

cards.front: Which jhsdb mode prints performance counter information?
cards.extra: It is the counterpart of PrintPerfCounters. --all prints every counter, which can be a very long dump.
cards.example:
jhsdb jsnap --pid 21891
# prints performance counter information

cards.front: In jhsdb jmap mode, what does --binaryheap produce?
cards.back: A heap dump in hprof binary format
cards.extra: It pairs with --dumpfile name to choose the output file. Without a dump file the binary heap would have nowhere to go, so the two options are normally used together.
cards.example:
jhsdb jmap --binaryheap --pid 1234
# produces a heap dump in hprof binary format

cards.front: In jhsdb jstack mode, what does --mixed attempt?
cards.extra: It only works where the platform permits it. --locks adds java.util.concurrent lock information, matching jstack's -l.
cards.example:
jhsdb jstack --mixed --pid 1234
# --mixed attempts to print both Java and native frames

cards.front: Which jhsdb debugd option sets the RMI registry port for a remote debug server?
cards.extra: It overrides the system property sun.jvm.hotspot.rmi.port, and defaults to 1099. The separate RMI connector port is set with --rmiport.
cards.example:
jhsdb debugd --pid 1234 --registryport 1099
# --registryport sets the RMI registry port for the remote debug server

cards.front: In jhsdb jmap mode, what does running with no option print?
cards.extra: The mode has a sensible default rather than erroring out. --heap gives the heap summary, and --histo the object histogram.
cards.example:
jhsdb jmap --pid 1234          # no option: same information as pmap
jhsdb jmap --pid 1234 --heap   # heap summary instead

cards.front: Why must jhsdb debugd set --serverid when several debug servers share a host?
cards.back: Each server needs a unique ID to be addressed
cards.extra: Clients then use server-id@debugd-host to select the right one. Without distinct IDs, remote connections are ambiguous.
cards.example:
jhsdb debugd --serverid srv1
jhsdb debugd --serverid srv2
# each server needs a unique id to be addressed as server-id@debugd-host

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::04 Monitoring and Troubleshooting

cards.front: What does jinfo print for a Java process?
cards.back: Java system properties and JVM command-line flags
cards.extra: With no options, both categories are printed. It is the quickest answer to 'what flags and properties did this running process really get'.
cards.example:
jinfo 1234
# prints Java system properties and JVM command-line flags

cards.front: Which jinfo option prints only the JVM command-line flags?
cards.extra: By contrast -sysprops prints only system properties as name-value pairs. With neither, jinfo prints both, which is often all you need.
cards.example:
jinfo -flags 1234
# prints only the JVM command-line flags

cards.front: Which jinfo option prints a single named VM flag and its value?
cards.extra: Without the value it reads; with it, it can write. For Boolean flags, -flag +name or -flag -name toggles them on or off on a live JVM.
cards.example:
jinfo -flag HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError 1234
# prints a single named VM flag and its value

cards.front: What does jinfo -flag +HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError pid do?
cards.back: Enables that Boolean VM flag on the running process
cards.extra: Writing flags requires the flag to be manageable. Many performance flags are locked at startup, and jinfo reports an error rather than changing them.
cards.example:
jinfo -flag +HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError 1234
# enables that Boolean VM flag on the running process

cards.front: Which jinfo option sets a VM flag to an explicit value such as MetaspaceSize=64m?
cards.extra: The = form assigns a value; +-name only toggles Boolean flags. Flags that are not manageable cannot be assigned mid-run.
cards.example:
jinfo -flag MetaspaceSize=64m 1234
# sets a VM flag to an explicit value such as MetaspaceSize=64m

cards.front: Which jinfo option prints Java system properties as name-value pairs?
cards.extra: These are the properties a running JVM resolved, including defaults jinfo adds, not only those passed with -D. Compare with the launch line before assuming a value was set explicitly.
cards.example:
jinfo -sysprops 1234
# prints Java system properties as name-value pairs

cards.front: Which extra JVM option might jinfo need against a 64-bit JVM?
cards.extra: It selects the 64-bit attach library. The same need can arise with jstack, so a 'cannot attach' error on 64-bit is worth ruling out first.
cards.example:
jinfo -J-d64 1234
# -J-d64 may be needed against a 64-bit JVM

cards.front: Is jinfo a supported, permanent JDK tool?
cards.extra: The same holds for jps, jstat, jstatd, jmap, jstack, and jhsdb. They may change or disappear in a future JDK, so do not build production automation on their output.
cards.example:
jinfo -help
# jinfo is experimental and unsupported; it may change or disappear

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::04 Monitoring and Troubleshooting

cards.front: What does jmap print?
cards.back: Details of a running Java process, e.g. heap histogram and heap dump
cards.extra: The most-used options are -histo for an object histogram and -dump for an hprof heap dump. Both connect to the live process.
cards.example:
jmap -histo 21891
jmap -dump:format=b,file=heap.hprof 21891
# heap histogram and heap dump of a running process

cards.front: Which jmap option prints a histogram of the Java object heap?
cards.extra: Adding live (as -histo:live) first forces a full GC and counts only live objects, which removes garbage from a leak analysis.
cards.example:
jmap -histo 1234   # print a histogram of the Java object heap
# the pid can be found with jps

cards.front: Which dump option in jmap -dump:format=b,file=heap.hprof selects the binary format?
cards.extra: It is the hprof binary format that analysis tools read. Without it the dump is not consumable by heap analysers.
cards.example:
jmap -dump:format=b,file=heap.hprof 1234
# format=b selects the binary hprof format

cards.front: Which jmap option prints class loader statistics of the Java heap?
cards.extra: It is the right tool when class loaders themselves are accumulating. By contrast -finalizerinfo lists objects waiting for finalization.
cards.example:
jmap -clstats 1234
# prints class loader statistics of the Java heap

cards.front: Why does jmap -dump with the live sub-option pause the application?
cards.back: It triggers a full GC to isolate reachable objects
cards.extra: That pause can be long on a large heap, and it changes what is in the dump. Use it deliberately, and expect a service-impacting GC on a busy production JVM.
cards.example:
jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=heap.hprof 21891
# live triggers a full GC to isolate reachable objects, pausing the app

cards.front: In jmap -dump, what is the difference between including and omitting live?
cards.back: With live only live objects are dumped; otherwise all objects
cards.extra: Dumping everything preserves unreachable-but-not-yet-collected objects. For leak hunting, live-only removes noise but loses evidence of what was about to be collected.
cards.example:
jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=live.hprof 1234   # only live objects
jmap -dump:format=b,file=all.hprof 1234        # all objects

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::04 Monitoring and Troubleshooting

cards.front: What does jstack print?
cards.back: Java stack traces of all threads in a process
cards.extra: For each Java frame it prints the full class name, method name, bytecode index (BCI), and line number when available. It cannot see native-only frames.
cards.example:
jstack 21891
# prints Java stack traces of all threads in that process

cards.front: What does the jstack -l option add?
cards.extra: It shows lock ownership, which is essential for diagnosing a deadlock or a thread blocked on a monitor. Without it, contention shows as the thread state only.
cards.example:
jstack -l 1234 > locks.txt
# -l adds additional information about locks

cards.front: What is the bytecode index (BCI) printed in each jstack frame?
cards.back: The position of the executed instruction within the compiled method
cards.extra: It corresponds to a line number when the class has line-number debug info. Without javac -g, BCI may be all you have.
cards.example:
jstack 1234 > threads.txt
# each frame carries the bytecode index (BCI): the position of the
# executed instruction within the compiled method

cards.front: What does jstack print for C++ frames with mangled names?
cards.extra: It does not demangle them; pipe the output to c++filt. This matters when reading native libraries such as a JNI binding.
cards.example:
jstack 1234
# C++ mangled names aren't demangled

cards.front: Why is jstack output on a 64-bit JVM sometimes incomplete or failing?
cards.back: The -J-d64 option may be needed for the 64-bit attach
cards.extra: Applying it lets the tool bind the correct attach library. The same quirk is documented for jinfo, and both stem from experimental attach code.
cards.example:
jstack -J-d64 1234 > threads.txt
# -J-d64 may be needed for the 64-bit attach

cards.front: Is jstack output stable enough for automated parsing?
cards.back: No — it is experimental and may change or be removed
cards.extra: For programmatic thread dumps prefer jcmd Thread.print, or the ThreadMXBean API. Human-readable text formats are intentionally not a contract.
cards.example:
jstack 21891 > dump.txt
# experimental format: not stable enough for automated parsing

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::05 Other JVM Tools

cards.front: What is the goal of CDS in HotSpot?
cards.back: Reduce JVM startup time by loading pre-processed classes and metadata
cards.extra: At initialization the JVM loads a fixed set of core classes regardless of the application. Storing that work in a shared archive skips decompression, verification, and constant-pool work.
cards.example:
String goal = "reduce JVM startup time";
String how = "loading pre-processed classes and metadata";
System.out.println(goal + " by " + how);

cards.front: What does the -Xshare: argument's default value do?
cards.back: auto — use CDS when a shared archive is present
cards.extra: Since JDK 12 auto is the default on all 64-bit builds. If the archive is missing or broken, the JVM falls back silently to normal class loading.
cards.example:
java -Xshare:auto -cp out App
# auto is the default: use CDS when a shared archive is present

cards.front: Why is -Xshare:on discouraged in production?
cards.back: It exits the JVM on any archive-loading problem
cards.extra: A missing, unreadable, or invalid archive becomes a hard startup failure. Default auto degrades to file-based loading, whereas on makes the JVM refuse to start.
cards.example:
java -Xshare:on -cp out App
# any archive-loading problem exits the JVM, so avoid it in production

cards.front: Which JVM flag generates an AppCDS dynamic archive when the application exits?
cards.extra: It records the classes the running application actually touched, giving a ready-made archive. Generating it has a noticeable cost at startup and termination.
cards.example:
java -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=app.jsa -cp out App
# writes a dynamic CDS archive when the application exits

cards.front: Which flag loads a previously generated shared archive?
cards.extra: This is used with dynamic and static archives alike. Pair it with -XX:+AutoCreateSharedArchive to generate or regenerate the archive when needed.
cards.example:
java -XX:SharedArchiveFile=<file> -jar app.jar
# loads a previously generated shared archive

cards.front: Which flag lets the JVM auto-generate a dynamic archive if it is missing or invalid?
cards.extra: Added in JDK 19, it looks at -XX:SharedArchiveFile and rebuilds when absent, corrupt, from an older JDK, or stale because a dependent JAR changed.
cards.example:
java -XX:+AutoCreateSharedArchive -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa -cp out App
# auto-generates a dynamic archive if it is missing or invalid

cards.front: Which flag dumps the list of loaded classes so a static AppCDS archive can be created?
cards.extra: That run needs -Xshare:off, otherwise CDS is already active. The resulting classlist is then fed to -Xshare:dump to build the archive.
cards.example:
java -XX:DumpLoadedClassList=app.classlist -cp out App
# dumps the loaded classes so a static AppCDS archive can be created

cards.front: Which two flags together create a static archive from a classlist?
cards.extra: You also pass -XX:SharedArchiveFile and -cp for the classes. Static archives include core JDK classes and support extra symbol and string data.
cards.example:
java -XX:DumpLoadedClassList=app.classlist -cp out App
java -Xshare:dump -XX:SharedClassListFile=app.classlist
# these two flags together create a static archive from the classlist

cards.front: What happens if the default CDS archive is missing when using a dynamic archive?
cards.back: Core classes load normally, slowing startup
cards.extra: A dynamic archive references the default archive location rather than copying those classes. With -Xshare:on the JVM instead exits with an error.
cards.example:
java -Xshare:auto -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=app.jsa -cp out App
# with the default CDS archive missing, core classes load normally, slowing startup

cards.front: What is the key advantage of a static archive over a dynamic one?
cards.back: It includes core JDK classes, so it is self-contained
cards.extra: A static archive does not depend on default.jsa at all. Deleting or corrupting the default archive therefore does not break startup that uses a static archive.
cards.example:
String advantage = "static archive includes core JDK classes";
boolean selfContained = true;
System.out.println(advantage + " -> " + selfContained);

cards.front: Which logging flag gives detailed CDS diagnostics during archive generation or loading?
cards.extra: The variant -Xlog:cds+lambda=debug adds detail on CDS's handling of lambdas. These flags show which classes and metadata actually made it into the archive.
cards.example:
java -Xlog:cds=debug -cp out App
# detailed CDS diagnostics during archive generation or loading

cards.front: Which flag confirms which classes were loaded from the shared archive?
cards.extra: Classes sourced from an archive report their origin as shared objects file. Others report a location such as jrt:/java.base for module classes.
cards.example:
java -verbose:class -cp out App
# confirms which classes were loaded from the shared archive

cards.front: Why is the generated CDS classlist file not to be edited by hand?
cards.back: It is a generated artifact whose format and comments assume no manual edits
cards.extra: Generate a new classlist by re-running the application under -XX:DumpLoadedClassList with CDS off. Hand edits make the archive diverge from what was observed.
cards.example:
java -XX:DumpLoadedClassList=app.classlist -cp out App
java -Xshare:dump -XX:SharedClassListFile=app.classlist
# the classlist is generated: its format and comments assume no manual edits

cards.front: Which classes can AppCDS archive, besides core JDK classes?
cards.extra: That breadth is why AppCDS delivers more consistent gains as applications grow. Plain CDS alone only covers core classes, and its benefit shrinks with application size.
cards.example:
String[] kinds = {"platform classes", "application-on-classpath classes", "application-on-module-path classes"};
for (String kind : kinds) System.out.println(kind);

cards.front: Which API do the bindings generated by jextract use internally?
cards.extra: That API covers foreign memory access and foreign function calls. It became a final feature in JDK 22, so jextract bindings target the modern replacement for JNI and Unsafe.
cards.example:
jextract -d gen mylib.h
# generated bindings internally use the Foreign Function and Memory (FFM) API

cards.front: Which jextract option sets the target package for generated classes?
cards.extra: Without it, the unnamed package is used, which makes the generated classes awkward to import. jextract creates the package directories under --output.
cards.example:
jextract -t com.example.generated -d gen mylib.h
jextract --target-package com.example.generated -d gen mylib.h
# sets the target package for generated classes

cards.front: Which jextract option names the shared library the generated header class should load?
cards.extra: A leading colon makes the value a path, as in -l :/usr/lib/libGL.so.1. Otherwise it is treated as a library name such as -l GL, resolved by the platform loader.
cards.example:
jextract -l GL -d gen gl.h
jextract --library GL -d gen gl.h
# names the shared library the generated header class loads

cards.front: Which jextract option adds a directory to the header include search path?
cards.extra: Include paths are searched in the order given, so -I foo -I bar checks foo before bar. This is how #include directives inside the main header get resolved.
cards.example:
jextract -I include -d gen mylib.h
jextract --include-dir include -d gen mylib.h
# adds a directory to the header include search path

cards.front: Which jextract option sets the output directory for generated files?
cards.extra: It is combined with -t to place the generated package tree inside your source root. Without output control, generated files land wherever the tool defaults.
cards.example:
jextract --output gen mylib.h
# generated files are placed in the output directory gen

cards.front: Which jextract flag dumps all encountered symbols so you can filter afterwards?
cards.extra: The dump can be edited down and re-fed as a plain argument file (with @). That lets you generate bindings for only what you need; large headers such as Windows.h become manageable.
cards.example:
jextract --dump-includes symbols.txt -d gen mylib.h
# dumps all encountered symbols so the file can be filtered afterwards

cards.front: Why do --include-* options on jextract act as an allowlist?
cards.back: Once any is specified, all unmatched symbols are omitted
cards.extra: The options are --include-function, --include-constant, --include-struct, --include-union, --include-typedef, and --include-var.
cards.example:
jextract --include-function glutInit -d gen freeglut.h
# once any --include-* is given, all unmatched symbols are omitted

cards.front: What happens if you exclude a declaration that an included struct depends on?
cards.back: jextract reports the missing dependency and generates nothing
cards.extra: There is no partial output. The dump-then-edit workflow makes it easy to accidentally cut a needed field type, so iterate until the tool accepts the list.
cards.example:
# args.txt includes an outer struct but not a declaration it depends on
jextract @args.txt -d gen mylib.h
# jextract reports the missing dependency and generates nothing

cards.front: How do you enable tracing of parameters passed to native calls?
cards.extra: It is a VM argument rather than a jextract build option, and the generated code prints the parameters as the call is made. Very useful when a native call crashes.
cards.example:
java -Djextract.trace.downcalls=true -cp gen App
# traces parameters passed to native calls made by generated bindings

cards.front: How can jextract reach a library written in Rust?
cards.back: Generate a C interface (e.g. with cbindgen), then bind that
cards.extra: jextract understands C headers only. For C++, an extern "C" interface works the same way, since many C++ libraries ship one.
cards.example:
cbindgen --output rustlib.h
jextract -l rustlib -d gen rustlib.h
# generate a C interface for the Rust library, then bind that C interface

cards.front: What does jextract --version print along with the tool version?
cards.back: The JDK it was built for and the clang version
cards.extra: Because jextract wraps the system C parser, the clang version affects how headers are interpreted. Mismatches with a header's compiler assumptions show up as odd parse failures.
cards.example:
jextract --version
# prints the tool version, the JDK it was built for, and the clang version

cards.front: If jextract is given several header files, what must you supply?
cards.extra: With a single header the class name is derived from the file name, e.g. foo_h for foo.h. Multiple headers leave no single name to derive, so the option becomes mandatory.
cards.example:
jextract --header-class-name Bindings -d gen a.h b.h
# required when several header files are given

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::05 Other JVM Tools

cards.front: What does jpackage produce from a Java application and a runtime image?
cards.back: A self-contained application image or native package
cards.extra: The image bundles the app and all its dependencies, including a runtime, so the end user needs no separate JDK. It can also wrap it in a platform installer such as exe, msi, rpm, deb, pkg or dmg.
cards.example:
jpackage --input in --main-jar app.jar --name App --output images/App
jpackage --input in --main-jar app.jar --name App --type dmg --output dist
# produces a self-contained application image or a native package

cards.front: Which platform package types can jpackage --type build?
cards.extra: The valid set depends on the host platform. If --type is omitted, a platform-dependent default type is created.
cards.example:
jpackage --type app-image --name demo --input in
jpackage --type exe --name demo --input in
# also: msi, rpm, deb, pkg, dmg

cards.front: Is jpackage cross-platform — can you build a Windows exe on Linux?
cards.back: No — each format must be built on the platform it runs on
cards.extra: So producing Windows and macOS installers requires CI runners for those OSes. There is no cross-compilation support for jpackage package types.
cards.example:
# build each native package on the platform where it will run
jpackage --type exe --input in --main-jar app.jar --name App   # on Windows, not Linux
# you cannot build a Windows exe on Linux

cards.front: Which jpackage options supply the application's entry point?
cards.extra: For a modular app use --module module[/main-class]; otherwise --main-jar plus --main-class. They are mutually exclusive, not additive.
cards.example:
jpackage --module my.module --name App --output dist
jpackage --main-jar app.jar --input in --name App
# the entry point comes from --module or --main-jar

cards.front: Which jpackage option overrides where output files are placed?
cards.extra: It defaults to the current working directory. The app's name and version come from --name and --app-version, which also shape the installer file names.
cards.example:
jpackage --type app-image --input app --name Demo --dest out
# --dest (or -d) sets where generated output files are placed: out/

cards.front: When does jpackage invoke jlink itself?
cards.extra: It builds a runtime image using --jlink-options and the --add-modules list. Providing --runtime-image skips that step and reuses your own image.
cards.example:
jpackage --input in --main-jar app.jar --name App
# no --runtime-image supplied: jpackage invokes jlink
jpackage --runtime-image myruntime --input in --main-jar app.jar --name App
# runtime image supplied: jlink is not invoked

cards.front: What are jpackage's default --jlink-options?
cards.extra: They trim the bundled runtime to what a shipped app needs. Override them only if you need debugging native commands or headers in the image.
cards.example:
jpackage --name App --input in --main-jar app.jar
# no --jlink-options given: defaults are --strip-native-commands --strip-debug --no-man-pages --no-header-files

cards.front: Which jpackage option adds alternative launchers via a properties file?
cards.extra: The properties file can set keys such as module, main-jar, main-class, arguments, java-options, icon, and shortcut settings. Repeat the option to build several extra launchers.
cards.example:
jpackage --add-launcher alt=alt.properties --input in --main-jar app.jar --name App
# name=path adds an alternative launcher via a properties file

cards.front: Which jpackage option supplies files to bundle into the application image?
cards.extra: Everything in that directory is packaged. Use --app-content to graft in extra files and directories from other locations without copying them into the input tree first.
cards.example:
jpackage --type app-image --input app --name Demo --dest out
# --input (or -i) supplies the files bundled into the application image: app/

cards.front: How does jpackage let you override bundled icons and templates?
cards.back: Put same-named replacements in the --resource-dir directory
cards.extra: Defaults differ per OS: .ico on Windows, .icns on macOS, .png on Linux. Installer-specific files like WiX sources or Debian control dirs live in the same directory.
cards.example:
# override/ holds same-named replacement icons and templates
jpackage --resource-dir override --input in --main-jar app.jar --name App
# same-named files in --resource-dir override bundled ones

cards.front: Which jpackage option passes arguments to the main class when the user gives none?
cards.extra: Values can expand environment variables and $APPDIR, $BINDIR, $ROOTDIR at run time. JVM-level flags go through --java-options instead.
cards.example:
jpackage --arguments "defaultArg" --input in --main-jar app.jar --name App
# default args passed to the main class when the user gives none

cards.front: What is the difference between jpackage --arguments and --java-options?
cards.back: One targets the main class; the other the JVM
cards.extra: Only --java-options can change things like heap or system properties, because those must be applied when the runtime starts. Wrongly mixing them yields arguments the app cannot use.
cards.example:
jpackage --arguments "alpha beta" --input in --main-jar app.jar --name App
jpackage --java-options "-Xmx1g" --input in --main-jar app.jar --name App
# --arguments targets the main class; --java-options targets the JVM

cards.front: Which Windows-only jpackage option is needed for an app that reads from or writes to the console?
cards.extra: Without it the app launches without a console window, so stdin/stdout interaction is invisible. On other platforms the console behaviour follows the launcher norm.
cards.example:
jpackage --type exe --win-console --name demo --input in
# needed on Windows for an app that reads from or writes to the console

cards.front: Which jpackage option signs the bundle on macOS?
cards.extra: Pair it with --mac-signing-keychain and the signing identity options. Entitlements come from --mac-entitlements, and --mac-app-store marks App Store output.
cards.example:
jpackage --mac-sign --input in --main-jar app.jar --name App
# signs the macOS bundle

cards.front: How does jpackage replace its bundled runtime libraries with a vendor's own?
cards.back: Replace them via --resource-dir, or use your own --runtime-image
cards.extra: On Windows the bundled runtime includes MS runtime libraries from the JDK. If a different version is required, the user must add or replace those files themselves.
cards.example:
jpackage --resource-dir override --input in --main-jar app.jar --name App
# same-named replacements there replace bundled runtime libraries
jpackage --runtime-image myruntime --input in --main-jar app.jar --name App
# or supply your runtime image

cards.front: Why must a macOS --app-content value be a directory containing a Resources subdirectory?
cards.back: Otherwise code signing and notarization of the bundle can fail
cards.extra: jpackage expects content laid out like the app bundle's Contents directory. A flat drop produces an invalid bundle that validators will reject.
cards.example:
jpackage --app-content MyBundle --input in --main-jar app.jar --name App
# MyBundle must be a directory with a Resources subdirectory, or signing/notarization can fail

cards.front: What does jpackage --temp directory change about cleanup?
cards.back: An explicit temporary dir is not removed on completion
cards.extra: Without the option, jpackage creates a temporary directory and deletes it when it finishes. Specifying one keeps intermediate output for inspection but leaves cleanup to you.
cards.example:
jpackage --temp build/tmp --input in --main-jar app.jar --name App
# an explicit temporary directory is not removed on completion

cards.front: How do you build a package from a previously built application image?
cards.back: Pass --app-image dir instead of inputs like --input
cards.extra: That mode turns an existing image into an installable package, and on macOS is also the way to sign a predefined image. Only signing-related and --verbose options are then permitted.
cards.example:
jpackage --app-image build/App --name App --output dist
# packages a previously built application image instead of --input

cards.front: Which option does jpackage use to associate file extensions with the app?
cards.extra: The properties file keys are extension, mime-type, icon, and description. The option can be repeated for multiple associations.
cards.example:
# assoc.properties: extension=.txt,mime-type=text/plain
jpackage --file-associations assoc.properties --input in --main-jar app.jar --name App
# associates a file extension with the app

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::14 JavaFX::01 JavaFX Core

cards.front: In JavaFX, which thread may modify the scene graph or update the UI?
cards.extra: All UI updates must be performed on it. Long-running work belongs on background threads with results marshalled back, otherwise the UI freezes.
cards.example:
javafx.application.Platform.runLater(() -> {
    javafx.scene.control.Label label = new javafx.scene.control.Label("UI update");
    label.setText("on the JavaFX Application Thread");   // scene graph and UI changes happen here
});

cards.front: What does ObservableList add over a plain List in JavaFX?
cards.back: It notifies listeners when the collection changes
cards.extra: JavaFX controls that display data expect observable lists and update themselves when items are added or removed. That is why a ListView needs no manual refresh.
cards.example:
javafx.collections.ObservableList<String> names = javafx.collections.FXCollections.observableArrayList();
names.addListener((javafx.collections.ListChangeListener<String> c) -> System.out.println("changed"));
names.add("Ada");   // unlike a plain List, listeners are notified of changes

cards.front: Which property does a JavaFX ListView expose for listening to the current selection?
cards.extra: A change listener on it fires on selection changes and on deselection, where the new value is null. Attach it once, then keep the detail form in sync with it.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.control.ListView<String> view = new javafx.scene.control.ListView<>();
view.getSelectionModel().selectedItemProperty().addListener((o, oldV, newV) -> System.out.println(newV));
view.getSelectionModel().select("A");   // listener sees the current selection

cards.front: In a ListView selection change listener, what is the new value when the user deselects the item?
cards.extra: Deselecting is done with Command-click on a Mac or Control-click on Linux/Windows. Clearing the form fields whenever the value is null avoids stale detail on screen.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.control.ListView<String> list = new javafx.scene.control.ListView<String>();
javafx.beans.value.ChangeListener<String> onChange = (obs, oldValue, newValue) -> {
    System.out.println(oldValue + " -> " + newValue);   // deselect prints A -> null
};
list.getSelectionModel().selectedItemProperty().addListener(onChange);
list.getItems().addAll("A", "B"); list.getSelectionModel().select(0); list.getSelectionModel().clearSelection();

cards.front: Which ListView setting enables selecting more than one item?
cards.extra: In that mode each additional CTRL/Command selection re-fires the listener with the most recent value. To get the full set, read getSelectedItems() rather than only newValue.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.control.ListView<String> view = new javafx.scene.control.ListView<>();
view.getSelectionModel().setSelectionMode(javafx.scene.control.MultipleSelectionMode.MULTIPLE);
System.out.println(view.getSelectionModel().getSelectedItems());   // more than one item can be selected

cards.front: What does a SortedList wrap, and how do you change its contents?
cards.back: An underlying ObservableList; you modify that list, not the SortedList
cards.extra: The SortedList cannot be modified directly. It re-sorts automatically whenever items are added to or removed from its backing list.
cards.example:
javafx.collections.ObservableList<String> backing = javafx.collections.FXCollections.observableArrayList("b", "a");
javafx.collections.transformation.SortedList<String> sorted = new javafx.collections.transformation.SortedList<>(backing);
sorted.setComparator(String::compareTo);
backing.add("c");   // modify the wrapped ObservableList, not the SortedList; order updates

cards.front: How do you keep a Compare-driven SortedList sorted when an item's fields change?
cards.extra: Changes to individual elements are otherwise invisible, so ordering goes stale. The extractor names the properties to observe, and those changes then trigger a re-sort.
cards.example:
class Person {
  final javafx.beans.property.SimpleStringProperty last = new javafx.beans.property.SimpleStringProperty();
  static javafx.collections.Observable[] extract(Person p) { return new javafx.collections.Observable[]{p.last}; }
}
javafx.collections.ObservableList<Person> people = javafx.collections.FXCollections.observableArrayList(Person::extract);
people.add(new Person()); people.get(0).last.set("Abraham");   // extractor makes SortedList re-sort on field change

cards.front: What is the alternative to an extractor when an item's sort key changes?
cards.back: Remove and re-add the item with its new values
cards.extra: A SortedList always re-sorts on add or remove, so the round trip fixes ordering. With an extractor, it is enough to change the observed property in place.
cards.example:
javafx.collections.ObservableList<String> items = javafx.collections.FXCollections.observableArrayList("b", "a");
javafx.collections.transformation.SortedList<String> sorted = new javafx.collections.transformation.SortedList<String>(items);
String changed = items.remove(0);
items.add(changed.toUpperCase());   // no extractor: remove and re-add with the changed sort key
System.out.println(sorted);   // SortedList re-sorts on add/remove

cards.front: Why does deleting by removing-and-re-adding an item keep a SortedList correctly ordered?
cards.back: Add/remove are the operations the SortedList observes
cards.extra: Element-level property changes are not observed by default, so the list has no reason to re-sort on an in-place edit. Add and remove are reliable triggers.
cards.example:
javafx.collections.ObservableList<String> backing = javafx.collections.FXCollections.observableArrayList();
javafx.collections.transformation.SortedList<String> sorted = new javafx.collections.transformation.SortedList<>(backing);
sorted.setComparator(String::compareTo);
backing.remove("b"); backing.add("b");   // add/remove are observed, so sorted stays ordered

cards.front: What do JavaFX bind expressions do when you call bind() on a property?
cards.extra: The bound property updates whenever any bound source value changes. This is what makes a Delete button disable itself as soon as nothing is selected, with no listener code.
cards.example:
javafx.beans.property.SimpleIntegerProperty a = new javafx.beans.property.SimpleIntegerProperty(1);
javafx.beans.property.SimpleIntegerProperty b = new javafx.beans.property.SimpleIntegerProperty(2);
a.bind(b);   // the bind expression reacts automatically when the source b changes
b.set(3);
System.out.println(a.get());   // 3

cards.front: Why can button.disableProperty() be bound directly to a selection model's selectedItemProperty?
cards.extra: A binding from a nullable selected item to a disable flag often needs a null test, so code usually binds to an expression like selectedItemProperty().isNull() instead.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.control.Button button = new javafx.scene.control.Button("Delete");
javafx.scene.control.ListView<String> view = new javafx.scene.control.ListView<>();
button.disableProperty().bind(view.getSelectionModel().selectedItemProperty().isNull());   // both are observables

cards.front: Before updating a model object in place, why temporarily remove the selectedItemProperty listener?
cards.back: A possible re-sort changes the selection and re-fires the listener
cards.extra: The listener would then reload the form from a different item mid-update. Immutable models sidestep the problem: replace the item instead of editing it.
cards.example:
class Ex {
  static void m(javafx.scene.control.ListView<javafx.beans.property.SimpleStringProperty> view, javafx.beans.value.ChangeListener<javafx.beans.property.SimpleStringProperty> l) { view.getSelectionModel().selectedItemProperty().removeListener(l);
    view.getSelectionModel().getSelectedItem().set("New");
    view.getSelectionModel().selectedItemProperty().addListener(l);   // a re-sort may change selection and re-fire l
  }
}

cards.front: What class tracks whether the user has changed any form field in the Person UI?
cards.extra: It is set to true on a key release in any editable field and reset to false after each selection change. The Update button binds to it so it stays disabled until an edit occurs.
cards.example:
javafx.beans.property.SimpleBooleanProperty modifiedProperty = new javafx.beans.property.SimpleBooleanProperty(false);
modifiedProperty.set(true);   // the user changed a form field
System.out.println(modifiedProperty.get());   // true

cards.front: Which FXML attribute links a control to its action handler in the controller?
cards.extra: It names the handler method, while fx:id exposes the control as a field for binding and lookup. Both are needed for a button to be set up and bound.
cards.example:
<Button fx:id="deleteButton" text="Delete" onAction="#deletePerson" />
<!-- FXMLController declares: @FXML private void deletePerson(ActionEvent e) { ... } -->

cards.front: In FXML, what does setting mnemonicParsing="false" on a button do?
cards.back: Stops an underscore in the label from becoming a keyboard mnemonic
cards.extra: With parsing on, the underscore marks the accelerator letter, so _File renders File with an Alt-F accelerator. Turning it off makes the label text literal.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.control.Button delete = new javafx.scene.control.Button("Delete");
delete.setMnemonicParsing(false);   // the Java equivalent of FXML mnemonicParsing="false"
delete.setText("_Delete");   // the underscore stays literal: no keyboard mnemonic

cards.front: Which layout control splits a JavaFX window into two resizable parts?
cards.extra: It divides the view, and each side can host its own container such as an AnchorPane. The master-detail UI pairs a ListView on one side with a form on the other.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.control.SplitPane split = new javafx.scene.control.SplitPane();
split.getItems().addAll(new javafx.scene.control.ListView<String>(), new javafx.scene.control.TextField());
System.out.println(split.getItems().size() + " resizable parts");   // two parts

cards.front: Which layout makes ButtonBar buttons all the same width, and how?
cards.back: ButtonBar itself, sizing every button to the widest label
cards.extra: Buttons in the bar align right by default. This keeps New, Update and Delete visually consistent without per-button width settings.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.control.ButtonBar bar = new javafx.scene.control.ButtonBar();
javafx.scene.control.Button ok = new javafx.scene.control.Button("OK"), cancel = new javafx.scene.control.Button("Cancel");
bar.getButtons().addAll(ok, cancel);   // ButtonBar sizes both to the widest button label

cards.front: Which layout arranges labels and fields in the Person form, and how is it structured?
cards.back: A GridPane, two columns by four rows
cards.extra: Text fields for first and last name sit in the upper rows, a notes TextArea beside them, and a single ButtonBar spans both columns at the bottom.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.layout.GridPane form = new javafx.scene.layout.GridPane();
form.add(new javafx.scene.control.Label("First"), 0, 0); form.add(new javafx.scene.control.TextField(), 1, 0);
form.add(new javafx.scene.control.Label("Last"), 0, 1); form.add(new javafx.scene.control.TextField(), 1, 1);
form.add(new javafx.scene.control.Label("Notes"), 0, 2); form.add(new javafx.scene.control.TextArea(), 1, 2);
form.add(new javafx.scene.control.ButtonBar(), 0, 3, 2, 1);   // 2 columns x 4 rows
System.out.println(form.getColumnCount() + "x" + form.getRowCount());

cards.front: What does a JavaFX record generate for its components automatically?
cards.extra: The components are final instance fields with accessor methods named after them. Records suit models that are immutable, such as a Person whose identity is its values.
cards.example:
record Person(String firstName, int age) {}   // accessors, canonical constructor, equals/hashCode/toString generated
class Demo {
    static void m() { Person p = new Person("Ada", 30);
        System.out.println(p.firstName() + " " + p.age() + " " + p.equals(new Person("Ada", 30)) + " " + p);
    }
}

cards.front: How do you update an immutable record model held in a sorted ListView?
cards.back: Create a new record, remove the old one, add the new one
cards.extra: In-place field updates are impossible on a record. Because add and remove re-sort automatically, no extractor is needed for sorting after an update.
cards.example:
record Person(String name) {}
javafx.collections.ObservableList<Person> people = javafx.collections.FXCollections.observableArrayList(new Person("Old"));
Person old = people.get(0);
people.remove(old);
people.add(new Person("New"));   // immutable: create new record, remove old one, add new one

cards.front: Why does a record-based model remove the need for an extractor in a sorted ListView?
cards.back: Updates replace the list element instead of mutating it
cards.extra: The SortedList observes add and remove, so it re-sorts. An extractor was only needed to catch property changes inside a mutable element.
cards.example:
record Person(String name) {}
javafx.collections.ObservableList<Person> people = javafx.collections.FXCollections.observableArrayList();   // no extractor needed
people.add(new Person("Old"));
people.set(0, new Person("New"));   // an update replaces the element instead of mutating it

cards.front: What must a JavaFX record model override for use in a ListView?
cards.extra: A ListView displays each item using toString(). Without an override, the record's generated form appears instead of the intended display text like a full name.
cards.example:
record Person(String name) {
  public String toString() { return name; }   // ListView displays this text for each Person
}
javafx.scene.control.ListView<Person> view = new javafx.scene.control.ListView<>();
view.getItems().add(new Person("Ethan Nieto"));   // the cell shows "Ethan Nieto"

cards.front: In the JavaFX theater metaphor, what does the runtime system create and invoke?
cards.back: The primary stage, then your application's start() method
cards.extra: You install the root node of a hierarchical scene graph into a scene on that stage. Menu bars are added directly to the stage and are only honoured there.
cards.example:
class Ex extends javafx.application.Application {
  public void start(javafx.stage.Stage primaryStage) {   // the runtime created this primary stage first
    System.out.println("start() invoked with the primary stage");
  }
}

cards.front: Where is the origin in JavaFX 2D coordinates?
cards.extra: The x-axis grows right and the y-axis grows down. That orientation differs from typical mathematical plotting, which trips up hand-computed positions.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle r = new javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle(0, 0, 20, 20);
// x=0, y=0 is the upper-left corner of the scene; x grows right, y grows down
System.out.println(r.getX() + "," + r.getY());   // 0,0

cards.front: Why is writing scene descriptions in FXML preferred over all-Java UI code?
cards.back: It separates the view from the model and controller
cards.extra: Each FXML file typically describes a scene and configures a controller. JavaFX also supports both 2D and 3D graphics, so the visual layer benefits from a declarative form.
cards.example:
<!-- Scene.fxml describes the view only -->
<VBox fx:controller="com.example.MyController"><Button text="New" onAction="#create" /></VBox>
// MyController.java holds the handler and model logic; UI structure stays in FXML

cards.front: What does the hierarchical scene-graph design let parent nodes do?
cards.extra: Each node is described by properties, and parents pass rendering down. That shared traversal is why a single property change deep in the graph suffices to trigger a redraw.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.layout.VBox root = new javafx.scene.layout.VBox();
javafx.scene.control.Label child = new javafx.scene.control.Label("leaf");
root.getChildren().add(child);   // parent passes rendering work down to its children
javafx.scene.Scene scene = new javafx.scene.Scene(root, 200, 100);
System.out.println(child.getParent() == root && child.getScene() == scene);   // true

cards.front: What are JavaFX transitions?
cards.extra: They animate node properties such as position, opacity or scale without a frame loop. Rapidly updating a property from application code is what the transition machinery exists to avoid.
cards.example:
javafx.scene.Node node = new javafx.scene.control.Label("move me");
javafx.animation.FadeTransition fade = new javafx.animation.FadeTransition(javafx.util.Duration.seconds(1), node);
fade.setFromValue(1.0); fade.setToValue(0.0);   // high-level animation of a node property over time
fade.play();   // no frame loop needed
